item.title: In Barcelona, Finding the Perfect Spot for Vermut and Snacks
item.description:
Spaniards really like their bars.

There are probably more bars in Spain per capita than any other European country, roughly one bar for every 175 people, according to a recent count.

And maybe no city in Spain reveres its bars as much as Barcelona. They are historical, cultural and usually, personal. Imagine Spanish “Cheers” and you start to get an idea. But in recent years, many of these establishments, known as bodegas — the kind populated by locals, with wooden casks of wine and vermut on tap — had been dying off.

The culprit?

“In two words: rents and greed,” said Ricard Martin, the food and drink editor for Time Out Barcelona. When rental laws were loosened around 2014, he said, landlords hiked rents that had long been regulated. Many bodega owners couldn’t afford them, sold off their licenses and retired. The places that opened in their wake weren’t aimed at inhabitants, but at tourists.

But as concerns about overtourism grew across the country, locals pushed back. In 2014, two local businessmen, Lito Baldovinos and Enric Rebodosa, bought one of Barcelona’s most forgotten bars, La Confiteria, to revive it. It worked: In 2015 the City Council designated the bar an “emblematic establishment,” which marks it as a business worthy of protection. To date, their company, Grupo Confiteria, has saved 15 establishments.

“What makes these bars unique is that they’re not designed as concepts. They’re the result of time,” Mr. Baldovinos said. “Layers of history, architecture, habits and people accumulate naturally.”

If you know where to look across the city, the bodegas are still there. Each bears their neighborhood’s fingerprint, but also shares a common trait: They look like they were decorated from a yard sale. Maybe there’s a trumpet on a shelf, or a painting of someone’s dead grandmother. Perhaps a framed picture of a sports team, or a black-and-white photo from a century earlier when everyone wore hats.

During a recent two-week stay, I wandered Barcelona in search of bodegas. This list isn’t definitive — think of it as a snapshot of neighborhood bars romantically stuck in the Barcelona of decades, maybe centuries, past.

On my first day out, jackpot: Bar Gelida in the middle of the Eixample neighborhood. Even in the early afternoon the bar was lousy with locals three deep. Its tiled walls and tall ceilings had a way of amplifying the conversation and the fluorescent, unflattering lighting. Gelida sits on the corner — which isn’t the usual 90-degree corner of most city blocks. In Eixample each street corner is cut at a 45-degree angle, or “chamfered,” creating octagonal intersections. The result is more sidewalk real estate to grab a table, order a plate of tripe stew and smoke.

Carrer de la Diputació, 133

Bar Bodega Gol, in the San Antoni neighborhood, is what you would get if you crossed a 75-year-old Catalonian bar with a loud, passionate soccer club. A handful of men were outside wearing Adidas track suits, smoking cigarettes and debating a match. Inside, the walls were lined with framed pictures of players, jerseys, trophies, pennants, soccer balls — everything but the pitch. Pity the person in an AC Milan jersey.

Every table was packed with glasses of beer and plates of pintxos: patatas bravas, calamari in olive oil, peppers, anchovies speared with a toothpick. (Bars, unlike restaurants, serve pintxos at room temperature.) People were speaking Catalan and Spanish, and laughing, eating, debating, arguing. Just not a word of English.

Carrer del Parlament, 10

El Pollo’s windows are perfectly positioned to take in businessmen, students and professionals walking outside, meeting up with friends at sidewalk cafes or jumping on their Vespas. I ordered a piece of Spanish tortilla, a glass of Verdejo and sat down to voyeur away an afternoon with my friend Kiki in the neighborhood of El Raval.

“We’re old fashioned in Barcelona. We believe that meeting people in real life is important,” said the owner Aimar Cordoba Bilbao. He has owned El Pollo for five years, but his ethos is loyal to a much older past. “It’s my grandmother’s recipe,” he said, pointing to the tortillas.

Carrer del Tigre, 31

Small and dimly lit, Bar Bodega Marin in the Gracia neighborhood has walls lined with wine bottles, casks and cases. Luis Sologuren, a Venezuelan man who bought the bar with his wife, Vanessa, in 2022, told me that since 1896 there have only been four owners. “In the old days, the usual customer was maybe 80 or 90 years old, and he would order one beer and sit on the same stool for three hours. It was not sustainable.”

Mr. Sologuren now serves food and sells wine, but a few old-timers still enjoy sitting on the same stool for the better part of the afternoon.

Carrer de Milà i Fontanals, 72

Technically, Bianco Noir, in El Raval, was opened by an Italian man and his French wife. But the décor, the lighting and the vibe are thoroughly of Barcelona. An ancient stone wall on one side, shelves of wine and liquor on the other, Bianco Noir feels like it hasn’t changed in a century.

The bar serves pintxos as well as larger meals like lentil stew, even bowls of pasta. “We don’t work to get rich,” said Christian Torlone, an owner, referring to bodega owners. “We don’t serve paella and sangria, the tourist menu.”

“I wanted to open a bar where people have a nice chat, enjoy a glass of wine, maybe watch a Barce game,” he added. “The bodegas of the 21st century have no soul. I wanted a place with a soul.”

Carrer de la Riera Alta, 8

Standing room only, line out the door, an array of food limited only by your imagination: This is the phenomenon of Quimet Y Quimet in the neighborhood of El Poble-sec.

When it opened in 1914, the bar only sold its own vintage but as the neighborhood grew, so did the bar’s offerings — eventually including a huge selection of wine, vermut and food. Shrimp with roasted red peppers, leeks with caviar, beans with cod, salted tuna with artichokes, anchovies with olives, some things glistening in olive oil, others dripping in honey, jamon in every form.

What didn’t change was the owner: Quimet Y Quimet has been in the same family for over a century.

Carrer del Poeta Cabanyes, 25

item.title: Where Future Champions Race Against the Tide
item.description:
The coastal road, barely wide enough for two-way traffic, wound behind the parish church and between fence posts and seagrass. My car shuddered along through a persistent, misty rain until the road ended abruptly, swallowed by an expansive stretch of beach.

I steered off onto a gravel lot, but the tractor-trailer behind me plodded ahead, jostling as it bumped from the road onto the sand. It was followed by horse trailers, trucks, tractors and, soon, hundreds of cars that parked in neat lines on the strand.

Beyond us, the ghostly outline of a racecourse stood out against the gray.

Each summer, thousands make this journey to Omey Island, a rocky, uninhabited spit off the Connemara coast in western Ireland that is only accessible at low tide. For more than a century it has hosted a day of amateur horse-and-pony races where aspiring jockeys, most of them teenagers or younger, compete against each other, and the tide.

The Omey Races are a treasured local tradition, but fleeting: When the waters come in, the racecourse is submerged and the island cut off once again.

The exact origin of the Omey Races is unknown, but they predate living memory in Connemara. Originally a gathering of farmers, the event was suspended for several decades starting in 1963 as Ireland’s agricultural sector declined, until a local committee brought it back in 2001. In recent years, the pandemic, maritime regulations and the whims of the tides have occasionally forced organizers to reschedule the event or cancel it.

But on a wet Sunday this month, the horses returned to the strand.

“It’s a big, big event for out here, on the island,” said Diarmuid Laffey, who grew up a few miles from the strand and helped revive the races in 2001.

He’s seen the island change, its population ebb and flow until the last resident died nearly a decade ago. But he said that preserving the tradition was important to this insulated stretch of coast, normally known as a burial ground.

He arrived at dawn on race day, joining neighbors to map out the course, set up neon yellow safety ropes and hammer stakes into the wet sand.

“Then the tide closed, came in on it,” Mr. Laffey said.

They watched the water rise to cover the rope and stakes, and waited for it to retreat again. As low tide approached, the races would begin.

The Omey Races belong to a broader circuit of amateur horse and pony contests that ripple across Ireland every summer, a sort of minor leagues for the island’s big-money professional racing season. The jockeys are as young as 11, the sponsors modest, the grand prize less than $1,000.

But the stakes for the participants are high.

“This is where the jockeys start off their careers,” Mr. Laffey said.

Caroline Mills, a breeder from County Meath near Dublin, said that contests like Omey help keep Ireland’s pony industry alive.

“Racing ponies are very hard got. They’re like hen’s teeth,” she said. “We sold a lot of them to England, because England could see how well we were producing jockeys.”

Many of the jockeys at Omey started riding for fox hunting or show jumping. But “the minute they get speed, it’s hard to go back to that,” Ms. Mills said, smiling.

Thady Finnegan, 11, was one of the youngest jockeys on the strand and making his debut at the races. The rain was relentless, soaking his white breeches and bright polyester jersey. He trudged to the weigh-in trailer clutching his saddle, his thick glasses speckled with raindrops.

Strapped to the back of a young racehorse, his face caked with sand, Thady tore across the course as the first heat got underway just after 2 p.m.

But it was a disappointing finish, and back behind the safety ropes, he took a moment with his horse to gather himself. “He doesn’t like to lose,” his father explained.

Thady, who grew up in England but now lives in Meath, began racing when he was 9. “I’ve never been here, but I’ve raced on beaches,” he said, goggles draped around his neck, his cheeks still red from the race.

His dream? “Try to get wins,” he said. “Try to be a champion jockey.”

For a few hours, the event brought all the trappings of a proper day at the racecourse to the strand: food vendors, souvenir sellers, a small grandstand and, of course, betting. Bookies ran makeshift betting counters from the trunks of their cars, huddling under umbrellas and hawking their odds.

Michael O’Riordan, a bookmaker from Cork, has taken bets at Omey, on and off, for a decade. The crowds are unlike other beach races across Ireland, he said, drawing former residents who had moved away and even far-flung relatives from the United Kingdom and the United States.

“A lot of people plan their holidays around it,” he said, then added with a laugh: “We might be able to take the American dollars home.”

In the open trunk of an S.U.V., Kian “Tubs” McNally, 16, and Camillus Byrne, 15, sheltered from the rain as they dressed for their pre-race weigh-in.

It was the final amateur season for the two teenagers, who will both soon be eligible to turn pro.

“I’ve been racing up and down Ireland every week for the summer, when you’re not in school,” said Camillus, who was competing at Omey for the second time. He planned to get his professional jockey license after turning 16 next month.

“You want as much experience as you can get before we get our actual license,” he said

For the two boys, what made Omey so special was the crowd. Through rain, sun, shifting tides and occasional downpours, thousands pressed against the ropes, watching and cheering.

“This is the biggest crowd there’s probably been in pony racing all year,” said Kian, who snagged the victory plate by a fair length aboard a pony named Buncrana in the fifth race of the day.

“The buzz when you’re cantering past in the race — it’s phenomenal. Everything about it’s special.”

Kian rattled off the names of jockeys who had raced the course in the past, many who went on to become champions on the professional circuit. “Please God, now,” he said, “if I’m half as good as them, I’ll be doing well.”

The last of the afternoon contests galloped across the course as the tide inched forward. The rain beat down with a gathering vengeance, sending the straggling spectators hustling for their cars. Soon, the strand would be emptied, the hoof prints erased, the tire tracks washed away.

By nightfall, it would all be underwater again.

item.title: As China Pushes to Expand in Asia, Trump Focuses on Iran
item.description:
It was the worst clash in years between China and the Philippines at a long-simmering flashpoint in the South China Sea.

For decades, the Philippines has claimed a small reef in disputed waters and signaled its control of the territory by rotating troops to a World War II-era ship grounded there. An international tribunal ruling a decade ago supports the Philippines’ claim.

But last month, a Chinese Coast Guard vessel began circling the ship, which is named the Sierra Madre. It was the latest in a long series of encounters between the two governments at the site, which is called the Second Thomas Shoal.

At one point, the Chinese Coast Guard used small boats to move in on Filipino service members and beat one of the men with a wooden baton, inflicting head injuries, according to Philippine and U.S. officials. China blamed the Philippines for provoking the clash.

The American ambassador expressed outrage and declared that the United States stood with the Philippines, the oldest U.S. treaty ally in Southeast Asia.

Yet no one expects China to curb its expansionist activities in the region anytime soon. And there are growing doubts among Asian nations over what the United States would be willing to do to deter China, given the enormous distraction and resource drain of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.

The United States is running low on critical weapons, including air defense interceptors. Iran’s missile and drone attacks have forced U.S. troops to leave bases in the Middle East and destroyed the sites, an indication of what the Chinese military — which is much more powerful than Iran’s — could do in a conflict in Asia.

In early July, China conducted a rare test firing of a nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile that carried a dummy warhead, sending it into the Pacific Ocean from a nuclear-powered submarine. It is one of the most powerful elements in its arsenal.

While China tests its might, President Trump’s State Department is closing consulates in Japan and Indonesia, according to congressional officials briefed on the decision.

Mr. Trump’s second term “has been a colossal failure for U.S. interests in the Asia region,” Representative Gregory W. Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement.

“This strategy, if you can call it one, is a gift to China that is undermining U.S. credibility and harming our national security,” he added.

Trump appointees say the administration is not ceding ground in Asia. In a speech in Manila on Aug. 10, Elbridge Colby, the under secretary of defense for policy, said the Trump administration aimed to “maintain a posture of deterrence by denial along the first island chain” — meaning it was willing to commit military resources to dissuade China from invading or attacking islands that include Taiwan and ones in the Philippines and Japan.

But Mr. Colby also said allies needed to spend more on defense and should try to integrate their militaries with that of the United States — and “not vainly and futilely seek to exclude or supplant us.”

Mr. Trump’s global trade war, whose targets have included Southeast Asian nations, has also revealed to allies and partners that the United States can be a commercial antagonist.

The U.S. government has lacked an economic vision for Southeast Asia for years, as Democratic and Republican politicians retreated from a Pacific Rim trade pact that President Barack Obama promoted.

That has left countries in Southeast Asia wondering what happened to the U.S. drive to ensure that it remains a presence that balances against China.

While Southeast Asian countries do not want to be trapped in a great-power clash between the United States and China, “they still want to feel the United States is a healthy counterweight to the P.R.C.,” said Mira Rapp-Hooper, who served on the National Security Council during the Biden administration and is now a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was using the initials for the formal name for China, the People’s Republic of China.

“So the perception that the United States is drifting as an alternative has also left a real impression on many of these partners,” she added.

While Mr. Trump has talked about China as an economic rival, he also embraced the superpower after it successfully retaliated during his tariff war last year.

During a summit in Beijing in May, Mr. Trump expressed admiration for President Xi Jinping of China, and he is preparing to host Mr. Xi at a state visit in Washington in late September.

Mr. Trump’s move to build what he calls a “G2” — Group of Two — relationship with China has upended a growing bipartisan push in Washington in the last decade to confront China as a hostile rival.

As the Trump-Xi bonhomie grows, some Asian countries are feeling left out, yet are also opting to stay on China’s friendly side.

That is especially true when China remains the largest trading partner for many of the countries, and the United States is not working on presenting economic alternatives.

“We’re in a very difficult position because you know we want to have that maximal relationship with both sides,” said Richard Heydarian, a political scientist from the Philippines. “And then for countries like the Philippines, it’s even more impossible because the U.S. is a military ally. We need the U.S. when it comes to the China threat, but the U.S. is not giving us much love on anything beyond the military aspect.”

The Biden administration agreed to work with the Philippines on expanding a transportation network, called the Luzon Economic Corridor, to better integrate the country into global supply chains.

The Trump administration is trying to bring the Philippines into its so-called Pax Silica initiative, with the notion of having the country work on semiconductor manufacturing and building artificial intelligence in a way that would benefit the United States.

But those nascent steps pale next to U.S. efforts to keep up its military ties with the Philippines. The two counties have long had a close relationship, and they have tried to maintain military cooperation, though their ties have shifted at times.

The United State made the Philippines its first colonial foothold in Asia after taking it from Spain in the Spanish-American War. And the Philippines is the only Southeast Asian nation that has a formal alliance treaty with the United States — one that requires their militaries to help with the defense of the other nation.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila last month during an annual forum of Southeast Asian nations that the U.S. military was determined to push back against China’s expansionist efforts.

“We’re never going to accept that international waterways are somehow under the control of other countries,” he said. “We’ll continue to sail through international waterways and freedom of navigation efforts of that kind, and we’ll continue to live up to our commitments — for example, with the Philippines and other countries — in terms of the treaty commitments that we have.”

During the Biden administration, the U.S. government took a hands-on approach to forging partnerships in Asia. It brought Japan into a security coalition with the Philippines. And President Joseph R. Biden Jr. got the Philippines to grant American troops expanded access to nine bases on islands near Taiwan.

In November 2022, Vice President Kamala Harris flew to the island of Palawan, east of the South China Sea, and visited a Philippine Coast Guard site there to send a signal to China.

The military cooperation has continued under Mr. Trump, despite the resource drain of the Iran war. In May, the U.S. and Philippine militaries tested a Typhon missile launcher at one of the islands, a public show with a weapon that could be deployed against Chinese troops if they tried to invade Taiwan.

The Philippines invited Japan to take part in multination military exercises in June, the first time since World War II that Japanese troops had been active on Philippine soil.

The move is both a continuation of the coalition overseen by the Biden administration and a hedge by the Philippines to broaden its partnerships beyond the United States.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: How Cyclospora Evaded the U.S. Food Safety System to Sicken Thousands
item.description:
Cases of cyclosporiasis were mounting rapidly in Michigan and state health officials were homing in on a common thread: Many of those who had fallen ill had eaten at Taco Bell.

On July 1, they asked the company for its supply chain records, crucial information in tracing ingredients that may have caused the outbreak.

On July 3, they wrote and asked for the records again.

On July 6, they wrote a third time.

“With the rapid nature of this outbreak and the number of people affected, we need to ensure we are completing traceback in a timely manner to preserve public health,” Lauren Edwards, an epidemiologist on the state’s rapid response team, said in an email to executives at Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell. (The New York Times obtained the correspondence under Michigan’s open records law.)

Later that day, Taco Bell provided some records to the state, which by then was working with the federal Food and Drug Administration. The F.D.A. asked for additional records two days later. Finally, on July 13, the agency received all the records it needed to pinpoint lettuce from a Taylor Farms plant in Mexico as a source of the outbreak.

A federal rule that had been scheduled to take effect in January would have required Taco Bell to send those records within 24 hours. But last year, the Trump administration delayed the implementation of that rule until mid 2028, saying companies needed more time to prepare.

Food safety experts say the postponement has hindered the response to the outbreak, the largest cluster in a record number of cyclospora cases in the United States this year.

“Time translates into illnesses and lives,” said Thomas Gremillion, director of food policy at the Consumer Federation of America, who reviewed the emails from Michigan. He added: “We would have had a much better response to this outbreak if they hadn’t delayed that rule.”

Cyclospora, which can cause explosive diarrhea, cramps and other severe symptoms, has been a recognized driver of foodborne illness for nearly 30 years. But this year’s massive toll — totaling more than 24,500 confirmed or suspected cases so far and two deaths — reveals shortcomings in the U.S. food safety system that may leave Americans more vulnerable to future pathogens, public health experts say.

Many point to an erosion of food safety oversight during the Trump administration, stemming in part from its aggressive efforts to roll back regulations and shrink the federal government. Last year, the F.D.A. laid off many of the staff who supported food inspectors’ travel planning and who coordinate with foreign governments on food safety. (An F.D.A. spokesman said on Friday that “travel support staff and staff that coordinated with foreign governments have been reinstated.”) The administration eliminated a committee tasked with studying problems that led to outbreaks. It also cut a program focused on cyclospora tracking.

“So far this administration has made our food less safe, not safer,” said Scott Faber, the senior vice president for government affairs at the Environmental Working Group. “By firing food safety experts, by reducing the number of inspections, by tracking fewer pathogens, and by failing to set up a traceability system that makes sure that we’re able to to clear the shelves quickly.”

Donald Prater, the F.D.A.’s acting deputy commissioner for food, said the agency responded swiftly with the information it had on hand. He added that even if the 24-hour rule had been in effect, it would not have made a major impact on managing this outbreak response.

An F.D.A. spokesman said that protecting the nation’s food supply remains a core responsibility, and the agency has the personnel and resources to respond to outbreaks of foodborne illnesses.

Taco Bell said it responded to requests from Michigan and federal officials in a timely manner. “We acted immediately, voluntarily and proactively to protect our guests and support health officials,” the company said in a statement.

On July 15, federal authorities tied the outbreak to iceberg lettuce that had been supplied to Taco Bell from a plant in Mexico owned by Taylor Farms, the large U.S.-based producer of fresh vegetables, fruits and greens. The next day, Taylor Farms began a recall of their products containing iceberg lettuce that had been shipped to 27 states.

A spokeswoman for Taylor Farms said it promptly responded to requests for information and is cooperating with health officials in the U.S. and Mexico. On July 19, it sent independent third-party experts to conduct a “top-to-bottom review” of food safety processes there.

Yet efforts by authorities to figure out how the iceberg lettuce in Mexico became contaminated by cyclospora, a single-cell parasite that infects the small intestine and spreads through feces, continue to move slowly. Although Taylor Farms temporarily shut down the plant on July 18, F.D.A. inspectors did not arrive in Mexico to inspect it until this week, nearly a month later.

The investigators from the F.D.A. were delayed in traveling partly because of clearances needed to work in an area deemed unsafe for Americans, according to a person familiar with the effort, who was not authorized to speak about it. They also needed to coordinate with the Mexican government and gather enough testing supplies to do a thorough investigation, the person said.

The slow start could make it difficult to discover a root cause of the contamination, said Sandra Eskin, chief executive of Stop Foodborne Illness, a nonprofit working to protect against foodborne pathogens.

Some of the problems that have hampered the response to this outbreak developed over decades: Scientists who study cyclospora said they have lacked the funding to better understand the parasite, including how it spreads and how to detect it. Food safety advocates say the goals of a landmark food safety law enacted in 2011 have not been met amid weak regulations and falling numbers of foreign food facility inspections.

The federal rule requiring companies to swiftly produce records in an outbreak investigation was drafted under that law, the Food Safety Modernization Act, which gave the F.D.A. new powers to keep food free of parasites and pathogens, to rapidly trace produce through the supply chain and to aggressively expand inspections.

The law set a goal of 19,200 annual foreign inspections by 2016. But foreign inspections have fallen markedly even as the foreign food supply has surged. In 2025, the agency made about 1,100 visits to foreign food plants and cited significant lapses in about 80 of them. Its last visit to the Taylor Farms facility in Mexico was in 2019, records show.

Even though finding the tiny cyclospora parasites during a site visit is challenging, such visits could reveal indicators such as irrigation water with high levels of fecal matter.

A spokeswoman for Taylor Farms said that it has a “robust fecal indicator testing program that includes cyclospora for all of our water sources. All of those tests have been negative.”

With the exception of the pandemic years, the F.D.A.’s foreign food inspections in 2025 were at a 15-year low, agency data show.

Currently, the F.D.A. has about 440 staff charged with inspecting more than 300,000 registered animal and human food facilities — domestically and abroad.

“Other things help ensure the safety of the food supply, but inspection is the classic consumer protection when it’s done correctly,” Ms. Eskin said.

Another major safeguard outlined in the law was meant to add visibility into the food supply chain, particularly for public health officials and regulators charged with limiting harm during an outbreak.

The rule that the F.D.A. ended up delaying last year was meant to “limit food-borne illness and death.” It required food sellers, including restaurants and grocers, to provide the agency or an authorized representative with a spreadsheet detailing their suppliers within 24 hours of an outbreak, or a reasonable amount of time the agency agrees to.

The F.D.A.’s decision to delay the rule was followed by action from the Republican-controlled Congress, which took additional steps to bar the F.D.A. from using its funding to enforce the rule and urged a revision favoring greater flexibility.

In Michigan cyclospora has now sickened more than 12,000 people and contributed to two deaths. Officials said in the internal emails, which were first obtained by Bloomberg News, that they had to contend with an antiquated disease surveillance system and analyze the information from interviews with 700 people who fell ill.

Once Taco Bell emerged as a common thread the interviews, getting the company’s supplier list was crucial, said Susan Mayne, a former F.D.A. official who remains active in food policy. In such a large outbreak, she said, it’s important to determine if one ingredient came from a central source, in contrast to those from an array of farms.

“The faster you can get back to the records, the faster you can identify the source of the outbreak and remove those products from the market and prevent further exposures,” she said. “So speed is everything.”

This week is not the first time F.D.A. officials flew to Taylor Farms’ Mexican processing plant to investigate a cyclospora outbreak.

In 2013, in the wake of an outbreak that sickened more than 600 people who ate salad at Olive Garden and Red Lobster, federal inspectors descended on the facility and examined more than 1,000 samples of lettuce, irrigation water and the feces of the farm workers, a main harbor for the cyclospora parasite.

They found virtually nothing, an inspection report shows. Every result was negative, except for one considered inconclusive.

The F.D.A. did note that the facility’s practice of washing the salad mix with recycled water had the potential to spread cyclospora, if it was present. But ultimately the agency could not “determine how or at what point in the supply chain” the cyclospora was introduced. Taylor Farms said it then began a new process for testing water and produce.

Jim Gorny, a produce safety expert who retired in 2024 from the F.D.A., said cyclospora wasn’t viewed inside the agency as high-risk like E. coli or listeria. Yet, some scientists were growing increasingly worried as cyclospora outbreaks grew in size and scope. Originally found in berries and basil, by the 2000s, it was affecting larger numbers of people after eating salad.

Cyclospora is a uniquely difficult parasite to detect, monitor and eliminate. Testing for it in the environment — especially in agricultural water — is extraordinarily challenging, and, as a result, rarely done.

Moreover, cyclospora does not grow in laboratory culture. Scientists often use culture as a tool to amplify tiny bits of bacteria, like salmonella or E. coli, to detectable levels. The same cannot be done for cyclospora, said Kalmia Kniel, a microbiologist at the University of Delaware who researches the parasite.

And because cyclospora are distributed sparsely in large volumes of water, finding them is like dipping a net in the ocean to find a single type of fish. There’s also no way to kill them in processing plants that wash produce like lettuce: They can survive chlorination, a standard process used to kill bacteria.

Dr. Kniel and other food safety researchers have been asking the government repeatedly for $10 million to fund work to develop new ways to spot the cyclospora in the environment and to set testing standards. But after four consecutive years submitting grant proposals to the United States Department of Agriculture, the work remains unfunded.

The U.S.D.A. said its peer reviewers had selected projects viewed as “most impactful” for growers and that it had supported some cyclospora research last year.

Dr. Gorny noted that he helped develop an F.D.A. action plan for cyclospora that was released in 2023. The plan called for increased and improved education, testing for cyclospora and rapid root-cause analysis of outbreaks. Recently, officials working on the plan held an educational session in a region of Mexico that had been tied to prior cyclospora outbreaks.

But progress toward solutions has been slow. F.D.A. guidance on produce safety released this week acknowledged that the agency does not know of any treatment the would prevent the spread of cyclospora “and be suitable for use on fresh-cut produce.”

As a result, there may be more summers of cyclospora.

“Until we get down to the hard work of better research, getting tools for better and faster detection and better root cause analysis,” Dr. Gorny said, “this is going to happen again.”

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi contributed reporting.

item.title: Summer Camps Strive to Stay Part of Canadian Life, Despite Hurdles
item.description:
This week my family participated in a quintessentially Canadian rite of passage: We dropped off our 7-year old son at sleep-away camp for the first time.

For the next two weeks, there will only be letters going back and forth between us. At least I hope he’ll write back — we stuffed stamped, return envelopes into his knapsack.

He’ll bunk with a few boys his age in a very rustic cabin with no electricity, and will be wholly free of screens. He can’t call home, unless there’s a real emergency.

He will fish, canoe, swim and — the best bit, according to him — learn how to use a knife for woodcarving.

My son has lived on three continents in his seven years, and watching him become attached to his Canadian life since moving here two years ago has been fascinating, and heartwarming. So when he came to us earlier this year asking to go to summer camp with his school friends, we took a leap of faith.

Parents I asked about the experience reminisced about core memories formed at lakeside summer camps in Ontario and elsewhere, and urged me to sign him up.

They told me about the independence the experience gives young Canadians, helping them develop foundational skills to navigate nature, water and the woods, safely, communally and enjoyably.

This, I thought, was about our son beginning to build the quality I have most admired in Canadians since moving here: grit — for him and, in some ways, for us, building our courage and trust in letting him go.

Grit is not necessarily a central goal in raising children where I come from. Greek parenting is focused on smoothing your children's way, making things easier for them. I attended overnight camps as a preteen and teenager, but they were not tech-free, nor were they as focused on nature. I called home regularly. So I got a few raised eyebrows when I told family and friends back home about my son’s Ontario camp plans.

Another telling reaction came from my father, when he heard the costs involved: “Are you sure you don’t want me to pitch him a tent in the olive grove and give him some farming work?” he jested. “It will be free!”

The cost of overnight summer camps in Canada varies, with the most affordable being about 500 Canadian dollars a week, and the highest-end ones 2,500 dollars a week or more.

Historically and culturally, the experience has been a building block of the Canadian middle class, but financial pressures on both the camps and the parents, and changes in regulations, attitudes and standards, have driven those costs up.

The Canadian Camps Association is the professional body that represents about 750 accredited camps around Canada that host more than a million kids a year, create 42,000 jobs for young people and generate up to 3 billion Canadian dollars in revenue. It identifies rising fees, pressures on family budgets and changes in parents’ attitudes as trends that can keep children away from overnight camp, and the organization is working with its members to counter those dynamics.

Information on summer overnight camp attendance in Canada is limited, but it seems to track U.S. trends, showing that camps have become increasingly expensive and are squeezing out children from less privileged backgrounds.

The camp industry has transformed since the 1990s, said Matt Wilfrid, the executive director of the Canadian Camps Association. He pointed to three major pressures: costly upgrades to water, sanitation and safety standards; post-Sept. 11 insurance spikes; and a shift toward more hands-on parenting.

But he added that Canadian summer camps are adapting, focusing on expanding access for more families from diverse backgrounds.

Mr. Wilfrid said that 80 percent or more of overnight camps are nonprofit, charity-led, religiously affiliated or otherwise subsidized. Several camps also serve children with specific disadvantages — for example, those with incarcerated parents.

“I never want a family to think that they’re priced out of the experience, no matter what type of camp,” he said. “You should always ask the camp if there’s any subsidies or bursaries available.”

The Canadian Camps Association is also lobbying the federal government to increase the tax-deductible amount for camp fees under the child care expense deduction benefit through a pre-budget submission, an initiative that Mr. Wilfrid said has supporters from across the political spectrum.

“We have a lot of members of Parliament that are champions of the camp experience in Canada from across the aisle,” Mr. Wilfrid said. “We can have very different beliefs on everything in Canada, but across the aisle, summer camp is this like beacon of hope and joy,” he added.

Matina Stevis-Gridneff is the Canada bureau chief at The Times. She lives in Toronto.

A petition to remove the U.S. ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, from his role is gathering pace, collecting more than 160,000 signatures since it opened on the Parliament website three weeks ago. The petition claims that Mr. Hoekstra should be removed because he is detrimental to the relationship between the two nations and has inappropriately interfered in domestic Canadian affairs. Mr. Hoekstra has been a faithful messenger for President Trump’s aggressive stance toward Canada and has a history of getting in trouble for eschewing diplomatic convention, but business leaders said they valued his attentive and frank approach with them.

Read the full article.

Ian Austen, our correspondent in Ottawa, reported on Canadian manufacturers and their response to Mr. Trump’s 50 percent tariffs, which are expected to be applied to a wide range of products, worth $20 billion, beginning on Wednesday. Some companies have been working tirelessly to fill orders and warehouses in the United States before the tariffs take effect. Others are reluctantly contemplating a move south of the border in order to stay in business.

Read the full article.

Norimitsu Onishi, The Times’s correspondent in Montreal, traveled to Umiujaq, Quebec, to report on the migration of beavers into Canada’s sub-Arctic. Drawn by a warming climate, Canada’s furry national symbols are colonizing new territory, evading Inuit hunters and reshaping the world they find.

Read the full article.

The stunning cottage made famous by the TV series and Canadian cultural juggernaut “Heated Rivalry” is only one of Muskoka’s treasures.

A Spanish health care company that pays people for their blood plasma is pausing operations in Canada months after two donors died in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Vjosa Isai reported.

Shania Twain, the pop-country megastar, has long had immense appeal. But as Lizzy Goodman, contributing writer for The New York Times Magazine, reported, an unlikely generation is connecting with the Canadian singer’s music.

An explosive wildfire in British Columbia’s Okanagan Valley drove more than 20,000 people from their homes last weekend and left one person dead.

A man was taken into custody in Nova Scotia after he communicated a bomb threat toward the U.S. Consulate in Halifax and flammable liquids were discovered in his vehicle in a nearby parking garage.

Passengers aboard a Porter Airlines plane headed from Victoria to Toronto had to wait for a flight the next day after a toddler remained standing in a seat and would not get buckled in.

A video of the Canadian pop singer Tate McRae using Neutrogena skin care products — with an ultralight touch — has led to a wave of parodies.

item.title: Quit Lit
item.description:
The book-tracking app Goodreads added a “Did Not Finish” (DNF) designation this spring so that readers can log books that they’ve put down or abandoned. The change, Erik Piepenburg reported in The Times, provoked an online debate: Is it a cop-out to DNF? As a reader who has been known to graze on books as if at a grand buffet, tasting a little bit of everything, I enter this discourse bashfully. I feel strongly that life’s too short to spend time on books one doesn’t like. But sometimes I wonder if the problem isn’t with the books but with me: impatient, seduced by novelty, impossible to satisfy.

When I told my friend Leigh that some people refuse to forsake books, she responded with outrage. “Why would you bother with a book you’re not enjoying? There are a million books,” she told me, as if I hadn’t sampled the first chapter of most of them. “This sounds like vestigial Puritanism.”

Indeed, but one needs to give a book a fair shake before deciding it would be punishing to continue. It takes a minute to engage with a book, to get a sense of the author’s voice and style, to understand what the book is doing. We like when books “grab” us, when they are “impossible to put down.” We’ve gotten used to the grabbiness of the internet, the posts and memes and videos that seize our attention and hold it hostage. I know I’m guilty of tapping out too early. I do it with books, but also with shows and movies. My attention struggles to distinguish between a novel and a TikTok video, between art and content, between being grabbed and being beckoned.

The most compelling reason to see a book through to the end is also the simplest: “It feels good to finish stuff,” one of the people Erik interviewed said. This is no small thing. Adding a book to my Completed list is incredibly satisfying. Even if I didn’t love the book, I’ve accomplished something. I’ve taken the journey the author intended. I’ve allocated my attention to something for a significant duration — a tiny modern miracle.

My friend Alice is one of the healthiest readers I know. She reads quickly and widely and is always ready with a recommendation. I figured she was a closer, a never-DNFer, the type to finish a book by hook or by crook.

“I could be 90 percent of the way through and I’ll dump it,” she told me, to my surprise. “I’ll dump anything! I’d let the fork fall from my mouth if I’m halfway through a dinner I don’t like.”

And yet Alice finishes more books than anyone I know. I never hear about the ones she abandons, because she does it quickly and without fanfare, without self-excoriation. She’s not keeping a public record of her DNFs, as Goodreads’s new feature encourages her to. Not finishing a book isn’t the same as never finishing a book. There’s no shame in putting aside a book that you don’t like, but finding a book that you do like takes commitment. You might try a few bites from the carving station or the chafing dishes, but eventually you sit down and eat a proper meal.

Politics

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to approve the construction of the White House ballroom.

President Trump dismissed concerns about the dire conditions reported aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, which has been deployed for months as part of the war in Iran. The deployment, Trump said, was “not nearly long enough.”

Federal officials spied on protesters, infiltrated group chats and obtained financial records as part of an unusual investigation into left-leaning organizations during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

Luigi Mangione

Luigi Mangione admitted that he shot and killed Brian Thompson, a health care executive, as he pleaded guilty to two federal charges of stalking resulting in death.

Mangione still faces a murder charge in state court. But his lawyers have filed a motion to dismiss it, saying it violates his legal protection against double jeopardy.

He faces the possibility of life in prison when he is sentenced in December on the federal charges.

Other Big Stories

Jason Arday, the former Cambridge University scholar whose remarkable career fell apart in recent weeks amid accusations of plagiarism, was found dead in London. He was 41.

Nigel Farage, the leader of Britain’s populist right-wing party, easily won a special election to reclaim his seat in Parliament. His main rival, a novelty candidate known as Count Binface, received 27 percent of the vote.

Google has enabled its A.I. chatbot for K-12 students using its popular Classroom app for schools. Previously, it had only turned the feature on for students 18 and over.

Film and TV

“Lanterns,” HBO’s next big bet in the DC universe, premieres tomorrow. Fans have been obsessing over star Kyle Chandler’s green ring.

Mary Heilmann, who achieved wide acclaim for her ebulliently colored, loose-limbed, often lopsided abstract paintings, died at 86.

In the sci-fi action film “The End of Oak Street,” dinosaurs invade a pleasant suburban neighborhood. It has “a sui generis oddness that’s rare in summer popcorn productions,” our critic writes. Read the review.

Christy Knowings, who starred on the Nickelodeon sketch comedy series “All That,” has died at 46.

In the video below, the director Jane Schoenbrun explains how the new film “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” uses conventions of the horror genre to have some fun. Click to watch.

Heists

The police in Brazil recovered eight works by Henri Matisse stolen from a library last year in a brazen daytime robbery.

The Italian police recovered another painting by Matisse, as well as works by Paul Cézanne and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen in a separate heist this year.

Theater

The Edinburgh Fringe is at theater’s bleeding edge, where its next great productions and stars often emerge. Here are eight shows from this year’s festival that have audiences buzzing.

Streaming has made theater a more accessible, more universal art form. Our critic highlighted some great performances and cast albums that you can enjoy from home.

More Culture

The stand-up Stavros Halkias has emerged as a counterweight to comedy’s rightward shift, while still remaining joyously lewd. He’s the guest on this week’s “Popcast.” Watch the interview.

RM, the leader of the K-pop group BTS, is contributing 145 pieces by Korean artists to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art this fall. He says collecting Korean art has helped him find his roots.

Phoebe Bridgers released her third album, “Lost Weekend.” It’s an emotional odyssey that shows off her songwriting powers, our critic Lindsay Zoladz writes.

By Melissa Clark

Embodying the “do very little to perfect ingredients” philosophy of cooking, this lovely melon salad with nectarines, tomatoes and basil from Hannah Shizgal-Paris of Roman’s restaurant in Brooklyn (as adapted by Ligaya Mishan) showcases the season’s best produce. The genius here is seasoning each component separately and building flavors gradually. Capers and pecorino provide bursts of intensity against the sweet fruit, while a squeeze of lemon ties it all together.

The Hunt: A pair of former dancers looking to put down roots in New York wanted a two-bedroom in Manhattan. Which would you choose? Play our game.

What you get for $480,000: A circa 1805 log cabin in Lexington, Ky.; a 1920 American Foursquare house in Pittsford, N.Y.; a Classical Revival house in Bradford, Vt.

Pick your favorite summer house in Iceland: Three two-story cottages offer scenic views and close access to mountains, glaciers and waterfalls.

Working with the landscape: On a hillside outside Birmingham, Ala., an architect saw a chance to create his dream house, which cascades down an incline.

Cottage country: Our writer was drawn to Muskoka, a Hamptons-like region of Ontario, because of its connection to the hockey romance “Heated Rivalry.” But it was the glistening lakes and weep-worthy sunsets that won her over.

Basket case: The must-have accessory of the summer? A Nantucket friendship basket.

Down the shore: A beach day should be carefree, so long as you pack everything you need. Here’s a roundup of the gear that five seasoned regulars never regret toting onto the sand.

If you live in a small space, you probably need to get creative to find enough storage for all your stuff. Don’t discount underutilized places: The backs of doors, for example, can be great places for miscellaneous items that fit into hanging organizers, like craft supplies, scarves or shoes. In the kitchen, use the backs of cabinet doors to hold lightweight items like aluminum foil or sponges. Hooks or magnets on the sides of the fridge can hold knives, paper towels or other small supplies. Finally, don’t overlook the forgotten areas of your home. The little nook between the toilet and the vanity, or the awkward upper corner of your kitchen, could be the perfect spot for random bits and bobs. — Caroline Mullen

item.title: Inside Russia’s Giant Push to Upend a Tiny Country
item.description:
It resembled in many ways a summer camp. Barbecues and beach volleyball games were on offer. A wellness spa was called “Relax and Have Fun.”

The men and women who attended the program at a resort complex in a remote part of Serbia also took part in more sinister activities, like learning to break through police cordons and set buildings on fire. They donned flak jackets and trained with assault rifles.

Their counselors, it turned out, were operatives with ties to Russia’s military intelligence service, known as the GRU. Their purpose, according to intelligence officials from three countries who described the activities, was to build a cadre of disciplined shock troops trained in election interference.

The target was tiny Moldova, a country of about three million people that carries outsize importance for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The Kremlin’s campaign included methods familiar elsewhere in the West, like hacking and disinformation. But in Moldova, its intervention went further than perhaps anywhere else outside Ukraine, and stands as one of the most extensive and audacious plots to date in Mr. Putin’s effort to destabilize the West, the three Western intelligence officials say.

Besides the camp in Serbia, Russian agents ran training programs in Bosnia and Moscow that were designed to turn pro-Russian Moldovans into foot soldiers. Moscow paid hundreds of Orthodox Moldovan priests to recruit voters and to push Russian narratives from the pulpit. And it spent hundreds of millions of dollars on a sophisticated vote-buying scheme financed by a Moldovan billionaire in exile and conceived and operated from Skolkovo, the Kremlin’s knockoff Silicon Valley outside Moscow.

Moscow’s campaign has not stopped. This spring, Russian missiles targeted energy infrastructure that provided service to Moldova, polluting waterways and disrupting electricity flows.

This article is based on interviews with activists who took part in the Russian effort; senior Moldovan law enforcement and security officials; and more than half a dozen European and American intelligence officials. The New York Times also reviewed thousands of documents related to Russia’s attempts to interfere in Moldova’s elections.

Many of those interviewed insisted on speaking anonymously, either to discuss sensitive security operations or because they feared retribution.

Details about Russian efforts in Moldova have emerged in court cases and local reporting, but the scope and extent of the campaign, including the vote-buying scheme and role of Russia’s intelligence services, has not been previously reported.

Publicly, Russian officials have denied interfering in Moldova’s affairs, and have dismissed accusations that Moscow is trying to undermine the West. Last December, Mr. Putin, in an address to military commanders, castigated European leaders for “stoking hysteria” over the threat from Russia.

Soon afterward, though, he gathered the leaders for a secret briefing to deliver the exact opposite message, according to officials from two countries with knowledge of the episode. Their goal for 2026, Mr. Putin told them, is “the collapse of NATO and the E.U. from within,” the people said.

Moldova is central to this effort. In the hierarchy of Kremlin priorities, the Western intelligence officials say, conquering Ukraine is first, and taking control in Moldova is second. Though it is not a member of the European Union or of NATO, it is strategically located, squeezed between NATO members and Ukraine.

Moldova would make an ideal beachhead for Russia for further aggression against either Ukraine or the West, the officials said, adding that Mr. Putin still hopes to conquer a swath of southern Ukraine to create a land bridge linking Russia to Moldova.

A map of planned Russian troop movements, publicly displayed by the president of Belarus early in the war, showed Russian forces sweeping into Transnistria, a separatist region in Moldova that hosts a contingent of Russian troops. Russia has not accomplished that goal.

Russia wants to use Moldova “as a springboard for hostile activities against Ukraine as well as its main defense and financial supporter, the E.U.,” said Stanislav Secrieru, the Moldovan president’s national security and defense adviser.

“For these reasons,” he said, “Russia allocated over the last few years unprecedented resources.”

The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The pro-Western government of President Maia Sandu has set E.U. membership as a priority, making it a Kremlin target. In every recent vote — including a presidential election and referendum on whether to apply to join the European bloc in 2024, and parliamentary elections last year — Moscow has poured in resources to dislodge Ms. Sandu and her party, PAS.

That was the objective last fall when Moldova held critical parliamentary elections to determine whether Ms. Sandu’s party would retain power, or cede it to a coalition backed by Moscow. The Kremlin had spent months preparing. Its cyberwarriors burrowed into the election commission; its vote-buying and propaganda campaigns were in full swing; its teams of recruits trained in Serbia were ready to sow chaos.

Sergiu Zama, a senior Moldovan prosecutor, who has been pursuing cases related to the election interference for more than a year, said just a handful of the recruits were needed to disrupt the voting. “The goal wasn’t to identify a thousand people to commit crimes,” he said. “Lighting the spark was enough.”

The Russians established their training camp at a resort in western Serbia in the summer of 2025, months before the parliamentary elections. The participants, mostly from Moldova, were paid $400 to attend a three- to four-day course, according to Mr. Zama — an enormous sum by Moldovan standards.

Videos from the camp, which Moldovan prosecutors and the country’s intelligence service said were taken from participants’ phones, show men dressed in camouflage and flak jackets training with assault rifles.

The Serbia camp was one of several established by Russian operatives. There was also a camp outside Moscow where more than 100 young Moldovans practiced “making and using incendiary items and homemade explosives” and handling drones “with special attachments for explosives or arson,” Moldovan prosecutors said in a statement. Two of the officials from Western intelligence services said the training was overseen by the GRU.

Iuri Vitneanski, a Moldovan political activist who attended the Moscow camp, denied that he had engaged in seditious activity. The purpose, he said in an interview, was to create “friendly, cooperative relationships” with young Russian politicians. He declined to say more than that.

He said he was unaware that the camp was overseen by the Russian intelligence. The Moldovan authorities acknowledged that not every person knew the camp’s true purpose.

Some attendees said they had refused to take part in training sessions. Maxim Rosca, who attended the training camp in Bosnia, later testified in court in Moldova that when he said he would not participate, a Russian trainer punched him in the face and knocked out a tooth.

In October 2024, three participants in the Bosnia camp were arrested crossing back into Moldova. They were carrying drone components, including attachments for dropping grenades, prosecutors said.

They also had a manual titled “Russian Cuisine: The ABCs of Homemade Terrorism,” prosecutors said.

The protesters gathered in the hot sun. They waved brooms and posters with antigovernment slogans.

The protest in the provincial town of Taraclia in July 2025 appeared organic.

Mr. Vitneanski, the Moldovan political activist who attended the Moscow camp, was at the event. In an interview with local television he described it as “the initiative of local residents.”

In fact, it was organized some 780 miles away in Moscow by operatives working for Ilan Shor, an Israeli-Moldovan oligarch who lives in Russia.

Days before the protest, Mr. Shor’s associates, using Telegram, the online messaging service, had reached out to thousands of Moldovans, promising them cash payments, and instructing them to show up at the town’s district council building with brooms, as a symbolic prop to “sweep these types away.”

“Travel expenses and per diem will be reimbursed,” said the message.

The messages were part of a massive trove of documents from Mr. Shor’s Moscow-based financial services company, which helps Russian companies evade Western sanctions. The documents contained names, locations and contact information for activists enlisted by Mr. Shor’s operation, and show that more than 150,000 Moldovans were recruited.

The documents also included hundreds of pages of chat messages among operatives working for Mr. Shor, whose username was Travolta.

It all added up to a sprawling operation overseen by Mr. Shor intended to influence Moldovan politics far beyond a single protest, Western intelligence officials and Moldovan prosecutors said. In exchange for cash, recruits were instructed over social media to post material on the internet and take part in choreographed rallies, urging Moldovans to vote against Ms. Sandu, her party and European Union membership.

The records were stored in a cloud folder belonging to a software engineer working for Mr. Shor that was publicly accessible on the internet and reviewed by The Times. The Times verified the database by contacting people whose information appeared in it, reviewing social media posts linked in the data and tracing GPS coordinates included in the database back to its developer’s address near the Skolkovo Innovation Center outside of Moscow.

After The Times contacted the developer in Russia, it was taken down.

Additional documents from Mr. Shor’s operations that were leaked on the internet showed payments to 38,000 activists totaling nearly $20 million over the four months in 2024 leading to the referendum on joining the E.U. The Times contacted some of the activists by phone to confirm their identity; others are publicly known.

The existence of the leaked documents and the material they contained were first reported by Ziarul de Gardă (ZDG), Moldova’s leading investigative news outlet. The documents have since been removed from the internet, but were provided to The Times by a person who downloaded them before they were removed.

Mr. Shor was well known to the Moldovan authorities. He fled Moldova in 2019 when he was charged with defrauding banks of $1 billion. He has settled in Russia, where, according to the three Western intelligence officials, he answers to Sergei V. Kiriyenko, a senior member of Mr. Putin’s administration who has responsibility for countries like Moldova that the Kremlin sees as in its sphere of influence. Mr. Shor’s company was hit by sanctions in 2025 by the United States.

Mr. Shor did not respond to messages seeking comment.

Using Telegram, Mr. Shor’s developers created 240 different chatbots to enlist and coordinate recruits, the database shows.

There was a strict vetting process to weed out “infiltrators” and police informants. New recruits were known as “sympathizers.” Above them were 35,000 “activists” and then, in the top tier, 1,200 local managers.

The operation grew like a pyramid: Nearly 99,000 members were signed up by someone already involved in the operation.

Mr. Shor’s operatives tracked progress with spreadsheets, which show Moldovan recruits posting thousands of messages to social media, denouncing the European Union referendum and Ms. Sandu. The recruits also promoted Mr. Shor, who, speaking in Russian, promised to provide Moldovans with free gas.

Russia is almost never mentioned. But one advertisement shared widely warns that closer relations with the West would lead to “an exact repetition of the Ukrainian scenario.”

“The result?" the advertisement said. “War. Death. Tears.”

Last month, the European Union imposed sanctions on four Moldovans associated with Mr. Shor’s efforts to undermine the 2025 parliamentary elections. Among them, was Mr. Vitneanski, who the E.U. said receives a monthly paycheck from Mr. Shor and was involved in “attempting to destabilize and overthrow the constitutional order.” The hacked documents show that Mr. Vitneanski received payments of about $2,300 each.

Priests were also enlisted in the Kremlin’s campaign. Hundreds of them traveled to Russia starting in the summer of 2024, visiting holy sites and senior church leaders.

Before they returned home, the priests each signed a contract for a debit card issued by a Russian bank, Promsvyazbank, which has ties to the country’s defense ministry and owns 49 percent of Mr. Shor’s financial services company. In the contract, a copy of which was reviewed by The Times, they declared themselves employees of Evrazia, a Kremlin-connected organization that Western intelligence officials said pushes pro-Russian policies in former Soviet states. Mr. Shor sits on the organization’s board.

In exchange for about $1,000, the priests were to urge their followers to reject the referendum on Moldova’s E.U. membership, as well as to campaign against pro-Western policies. Hundreds took the cash, Moldovan officials said.

The hacked documents described one priest, the Rev. Gheorghe Tursulet, as “a reliable asset,” and records a payment of about $1,000. A senior Moldovan official confirmed that he participated in the pilgrimages to Russia.

Another Moldovan priest, the Rev. Pavel Petrov, is affiliated with a group of pro-Russian priests but did not attend the pilgrimages, the senior official said. A few weeks before the 2024 election he delivered remarks from the pulpit denouncing the E.U.

“Democracy? What kind of democracy imposes on you all the filth they brought from Europe?” he asked, going on to decry schools with mix-gendered bathrooms.

“We, the people, what do we want? Sodom and Gomorrah? For God to burn us alive? He will burn us,” he said according to cellphone video of his sermon, which was later published by a local new outlet, NordNews, and verified by The Times.

Father Tursulet and Father Petrov did not respond to a request for comment.

The Rev. Iulian Rața, the archpriest of the town of Orhei, insisted in an interview that neither he nor the priests he oversees “conducted a direct campaign or supported anyone in elections.”

Even so, he is an unapologetic opponent of Ms. Sandu’s government, which he has accused of harassing priests like him who are loyal to the Russian Orthodox Church. He acknowledged participating in the pilgrimages to Moscow and said he would do it again. Politics, he said, would shift back in his favor.

“We’ll wait,” he said. “They have two years until the next elections.”

The Russians almost pulled it off.

On the day of parliamentary elections, Sept. 28, 2025, they brought together all of their efforts.

Operatives trained in Serbia prepared to cause chaos in Chisinau and elsewhere. They wore yellow and blue armbands to distinguish one another in the crowds, according to Mr. Zama, the prosecutor. Some carried incendiary devices, he said.

Russian hackers had penetrated Moldova’s Central Election Commission, and took over thousands of personal routers, the senior Moldovan official said.

The Moldovan authorities were prepared.

In the weeks before the vote, the Moldovan police conducted raids on hundreds of homes, arresting people who had attended the camps or had taken money as part of Mr. Shor’s scheme.

Moldova’s cyberexperts, aided by Western allies, stymied the hacking attacks. Protests broke out, but there was no serious violence.

When the police arrested several people suspected of plotting violence, those arrested claimed that incendiary devices in their possession were meant for a gender reveal party, Mr. Zama said.

Ms. Sandu’s party squeaked by with just over 50 percent of the vote, largely on the strength of the Moldovan diaspora abroad.

For the Kremlin, her victory was hardly a failure. The Moldovan government had to spend a small fortune and devote vast law enforcement resources to thwart the Russian interference. And the Kremlin’s allies have used the mass arrests of Ms. Sandu’s opponents for propaganda purposes, presenting it as proof of an authoritarian crackdown.

The Kremlin has since expanded its efforts.

In early March, a Russian attack on a Ukrainian hydroelectric plant near the border with Moldova contaminated the water supply for a swath of Ukraine and Moldova.

Then Russian drones hit a high voltage line in western Ukraine that provides up to 70 percent of Moldova’s electricity, leading to blackouts. When we visited some government buildings, including the presidential complex, the lights were often turned off to conserve power and workers traversed windowless hallways with flashlights.

Moscow, Moldovan officials said, is playing a long game.

“We won the battle,” said Mihai Lupascu, the director of Moldova’s Agency for Cybersecurity. “But we did not win the war.”

Julian E. Barnescontributed reporting from Washington, and Anna Moghilda from Chisinau, Moldova.

item.title: Heat Deaths in a ‘Cold’ Country Are a Warning to the Rest of Europe
item.description:
Seniors died in stifling apartments. Emergency calls were left on hold. Doctors treated an onslaught of people sick from heat, sometimes in wards without air-conditioning.

These are scenes that played out in Belgium, one of the world’s wealthiest nations, on a recent summer weekend. They are also a warning to Europe.

Europe is the fastest-warming continent, yet large parts remain ill prepared. As heat waves scorch its nations this summer, they are killing thousands in countries with strong health systems. In just one week in late June, there were around 16,000 excess deaths, or more people who died than usual, in Europe. Belgium, France and Germany were the worst affected, based on data collected by the European Mortality Monitoring Network.

Belgium, known for cold and damp, not searing heat, had the highest excess deaths in Europe, making it a case study into what went wrong. In Wallonia, the region that makes up the country’s south, the death rate was 77 percent higher than what would be expected between mid-June and early July. Some hospitals were overrun, with gurneys and patients lining the hallways and medical staff working without breaks in the unrelenting heat.

“Each crisis is becoming increasingly severe,” said Yves Coppieters, the health minister for Wallonia. “That’s what we’re failing to anticipate.”

Expected range

Sources: StatBel (daily deaths); Sciensano (typical range). Josh Holder/The New York Times

Climate change means that the issue is most likely here to stay. Across Europe, “we think the summers are hot now,” said Joan Ballester Claramunt, a research professor at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health who focuses on climate change and health. “The future that we’re seeing, it could be much worse.”

Belgium is a stark example of why heat waves can become deadly in countries more accustomed to cool weather. Emergency systems in some cases buckled under the pressure, and structural challenges left the most vulnerable to suffer.

The federal health ministry defended elements of the response and noted that hospital capacity had been scaled up during the crisis, but it acknowledged that some change was needed. “I believe we must indeed learn lessons quickly,” Frank Vandenbroucke, the Belgian minister of social affairs and public health, told lawmakers early last month.

During the late June wave, MontLégia hospital, in the Belgian city of Liège, experienced a rush of patients so intense that in the emergency room healthier people were temporarily lined up in hallways so that those past the point of saving could have privacy while they died.

Dr. Arnaud Detroz, who was working that weekend, said his team was confronted with overheating cases that they had seen mostly in textbooks. “In our countries, at our latitudes, these cases are relatively rare,” he said.

Belgium is not accustomed to taking heat so seriously.

At the start of the June heat wave, Theo Francken, the defense minister, posted an image on Instagram of himself smiling in the sun with the caption, “It’s warm for two days and we’re all going to die again apparently.” He criticized the press.

“Enjoy the beautiful weather,” he added. “And LIVE!”

The weather quickly turned into a matter of life or death.

Temperatures shot up between mid-June and early July, surpassing 100 degrees in parts of Wallonia. The fact that it was early in the summer, before people had a chance to acclimatize, worsened the danger, experts said.

In the last weekend of June, the Belgian emergency call line was severely overwhelmed, according to medical groups whose representatives signed an open letter protesting the meltdown. In some cases, they said, it took 10 minutes just to get through to an operator. (Bernard Quintin, the Belgian interior minister, told lawmakers that average waits were much shorter and noted that extra staff members were brought in.)

“If you have to wait for 10 minutes if you have a stroke or heart attack, it’s quite a big problem,” said Dr. Pierre-Louis Deudon, a general practitioner in the Brussels region who signed the letter.

Deaths spiked in northwest Europe in June, where countries were unprepared for extreme heat that hit much of the continent.

Emergency rooms were also overrun in parts of Wallonia. During the peak of the heat wave, the number of emergency vehicles arriving at Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, about an hour’s drive west of Liège, rose from an average of 60 to up to 110 per day, said Dr. Laurent Peyskens, deputy head of the emergency department.

“It was very crushing,” Dr. Peyskens said.

Half of all emergency rooms in Wallonia lacked air-conditioning, said Dr. Phillippe Devos, director general at Unessa, a federation of Belgian health care providers in Brussels and Wallonia.

For Belgium, June 27 appears to have been the second-deadliest day of the 21st century, after a day early in the coronavirus crisis. In Wallonia, June 28 was deadlier than the depths of the pandemic in 2020.

“We should definitely be afraid of a repeat,” said Loïc Gillerot, a climate-health expert at CERAC, an independent Belgian research center that studies climate risk. “The question is: Are we talking about a repeat this summer?”

In Belgium, as elsewhere, extreme heat hit the vulnerable the hardest.

The region of Wallonia had more than twice as much excess mortality as the northern region of Flanders.

Part of the problem, experts said, is that people in Wallonia have lower incomes on average. Poor people are more likely to have pre-existing health conditions, and they often lack access to well-ventilated housing.

About 85 percent of the more than 900 excess deaths in Wallonia between mid-June and July 1 were of people 65 or older, according to figures from Sciensano, the Belgian health data institute. Low-income seniors who lived alone were particularly at risk, health care professionals said, as their houses or attic apartments became baking death traps.

“You have people who are isolated, old,” Dr. Devos said. “We saw in the emergency rooms: When people came to the E.R., it was impossible to save them.”

Wallonia’s housing was part of the challenge. Many residential buildings are aging and were constructed to hold in heat, not to keep it out.

“It’s a country that is considered cold, culturally,” said Gilles Vanvolsem, managing director of the Belgian Green Building Council. “People think more about heating their house than cooling their house.”

Nor did behaviors adjust. Belgians, including those with medical conditions and their caregivers, at times appeared unaware of how to handle the heat.

Dr. Deudon in Brussels noted, for instance, that people on antidepressants and other mental health drugs often are not made aware that they are at higher risk, and so they continued to go to work as normal.

Dr. Toon Ceyssens, a general practitioner in Flanders, echoed that concern, noting that blood pressure medications also increase the danger.

During the worst of the heat wave, he was alarmed to see residents at a care institution where he works still taking excursions. “The caretakers and the patients didn’t take the heat wave that seriously,” he said.

To limit heat risk, countries like Belgium will need to shake their cold-country mentality, experts said.

Dr. Ceyssens said patients were often hesitant to install air-conditioning, worried that it would make them sick, spread germs and harm the environment.

Belgians do not “want to be Americans,” with the indoor temperature set to 65 degrees, he said, but he saw a middle ground in which vulnerable people would have access.

“The mentality on air-conditioning has to change,” he said.

Others disagree. Even some Belgian officials are wary of relying too much on climate control, concerned that adding it could overwhelm the power grid and leave cities even hotter by pumping hot air into the streets.

“Air-conditioning can be appropriate in specific situations, particularly for vulnerable people or certain buildings,” said Simon Souris, a spokesman for Wallonia’s housing and energy minister. “However, our long-term strategy is not based on its widespread deployment.”

Since June, Belgian experts have issued recommendations for more cooling spaces and resources for the vulnerable. Federal authorities are working toward handling emergency calls differently, doctors said. The housing authorities in Wallonia are instituting policies to encourage housing renovation.

Yet medical workers and public health experts fear that the kind of changes that are needed — like housing and infrastructure improvements — will take more time than Belgium has. At MontLégia, doctors remain concerned that officials will not dedicate enough resources to the ongoing threat of heat.

Late last month, as emergency doctors recalled losing patients in June, another arrived.

A 77-year-old woman was wheeled in with heat stroke, her frail chest heaving, her temperature near the point of organ failure. Doctors cut off her blouse and covered her in ice packs.

They are bracing for more. A supply closet on the emergency-room floor is stocked with fans. Nearby, a refrigerator is filled with cooling IV drips.

“As emergency-room doctors, we can come to terms with fatality, but it’s not the same when you know it’s due to a systemic failure,” said Dr. Michèle Yerna, who runs the MontLégia emergency unit. That, she added, is “much harder to bear.”
