item.title: Entrenched, Embattled and Defiant, the Taliban Celebrate 5 Years in Power
item.description:
The black and white flags of the Taliban were flying high along the streets of Kabul, Afghanistan’s capital, as the group celebrated five years in power on Saturday.

Shiny Mercedes-Benzes drove casually in front of graffiti praising the Taliban fighters’ “sacrifice,” the word painted in crimson, with depictions of drops of blood. Young Afghans chanted independence songs below posters hailing how “the carpet of democracy” had been removed for Islamic rule.

But the triumphant tone is only half the story. The Taliban may be boisterous in Kabul and have a tight grip on power, yet elsewhere they find themselves targeted and face crises both at home and abroad.

They face a conflict just short of open war with neighboring Pakistan. They’re dealing with new waves of attacks from armed groups that want to topple them. Add to that mass unemployment, international isolation and growing domestic discontent, and the Taliban face their most serious threats since their return to power in 2021.

It is too early to tell whether all those challenges will escalate and threaten their survival as a governing force. And as the scenes of celebration on Saturday showed, the Taliban are popular among many.

Still, the threats they face have cracked the veneer of security and stability that the Taliban have heralded as their primary achievement — and their main selling point to the world.

As workers were preparing Kabul for celebrations on Thursday, a resistance group claimed responsibility for the killing of the Taliban mayor of a provincial capital in northern Afghanistan. Two weeks earlier, another Taliban official had been assassinated in the same province.

The Taliban are holding Afghan society in a chokehold that spares no one. Girls and women face restrictions to a degree unseen anywhere else in the world. Religious minorities are witnessing the forced closure of their places of worship. Anyone who voices criticism is repressed. United Nations staff members face arrests; journalists and rights workers suffer forced disappearances.

The Taliban are collecting taxes and building roads, dams and canals. European countries have welcomed them in Brussels to facilitate the deportation of Afghan migrants and asylum seekers. They have expanded trade ties with Central Asian states and want the Trump administration to come back to Afghanistan.

Whenever a sign of dissent emerges in a province, the country’s secretive and ultraconservative leader, Sheikh Haibatullah Akhundzada, places a key ally in a leadership position to keep things in check.

And yet the signs of trouble that have appeared in recent months are impossible to ignore.

Sporadic sounds of gunfire reverberated across the remote mountains of northeastern Afghanistan on a recent evening. Weary Taliban fighters peppered drivers with questions at checkpoints dotting the main road snaking through the province of Badakhshan.

On the same road, two attackers had killed a senior provincial Talib official a week earlier. A small group of anti-Taliban fighters had briefly seized control of a police headquarters in a nearby district.

Now fighting between the Taliban and another group opposing their rule was continuing in another district of Badakhshan. The province, bordering China, Pakistan and Tajikistan, is emerging as a hot spot.

On a trip to the province this month, we talked to residents ready to support anti-Taliban groups because they said they were fed up with the Taliban’s iron grip, the lack of job opportunities and the government’s confiscation of natural resources.

We drove through dozens of checkpoints and witnessed the heavy presence of intelligence officers in the isolated village where anti-Taliban fighters had stormed police headquarters.

The clashes and the attacks have so far been scattered. The leader of one of the anti-Taliban groups described them as “opportunity targets” aimed at challenging the Taliban’s sense of control. But the leader, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the group’s strategy, said the number of attacks would only increase in coming months.

An underequipped Afghan Army waits nervously at the border with Pakistan. Once a sponsor of the Taliban, Pakistan has launched dozens of airstrikes on Afghanistan, killing 500 civilians since October, according to the United Nations, and has threatened to use even more force if the Taliban don’t rein in militants who are staging attacks on Pakistani territory.

The mistrust goes both ways: The Taliban have accused Pakistan of supporting the armed groups that have attacked Taliban outposts in Badakhshan.

Whether, or to what extent, Pakistan is actively supporting anti-Taliban groups is not clear, but suspicions are running high.

“The Pakistanis are happy to be portrayed now as a potential patron for the armed opposition to the Taliban, because that increases their leverage over the group,” said Fabrizio Foschini, a researcher at the Afghanistan Analysts Network.

The picture on the domestic front is also grim. Extreme hunger has been spreading fast from one province to another after aid cuts last year plunged millions into deeper food insecurity. The Taliban’s ban on secondary and university education for women and girls is stifling development, experts say.

The Taliban have deprived 2.4 million Afghan girls of an education, according to UNESCO — the equivalent of all school-age girls in New York, Mexico City and Moscow combined — forced to stay home indefinitely.

Some scattered signs of discontent have popped up. At a rare protest in June, demonstrators chanted “Work, education, freedom,” similar to what their Iranian neighbors chanted in 2022. And the leader of a large religious minority warned the Taliban in May: Don’t squeeze Afghan society too much, or it will explode.

The Taliban know the world wants a stable Afghanistan — one that isn’t a source of refugees, drugs or terrorism.

They assert that the country no longer poses a security threat to the region or the West. They say that they have cracked down on the Islamic State, and that they want peaceful relations, based on trade and diplomacy, including with the U.S.

Since the Taliban no longer carry out suicide attacks, bomb schools or target the security forces they now represent, their main argument may hold.

“The greatest achievement we have had over the past five years is security,” Afghanistan’s foreign minister, Amir Khan Muttaqi, said in an interview with The New York Times in Kabul on Wednesday.

They don’t want their various crises to spiral either.

All the ingredients for things to get out of control in Afghanistan again are here, analysts say: A vast population of unemployed young Afghans are fertile ground for radicalization, especially as economic opportunities are nearly nonexistent. And with animosity growing between Pakistan and Afghanistan, it is unclear who might come to the Taliban’s aid: Afghanistan is, once again, a pariah state, with barely any allies.

The past five years have brought some predictability and an end to almost two decades of fighting, which many Afghans have welcomed, despite the immense hardship and repression. But the country remains shattered, and the fragile peace is already at risk.

item.title: At Least 20 Dead as 7.7-Magnitude Earthquake Rocks Indonesia
item.description:
At least 20 people were killed on Saturday after a 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck just off the coast of an island in eastern Indonesia, officials said.

The earthquake hit north of Flores Island, the United States Geological Survey said. It caused several buildings to collapse on the island, and was one of the largest the area had experienced in decades, said Wijayanto, the director of earthquake and tsunami affairs at the Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency in Indonesia.

“An earthquake like this occurred in 1992 with a magnitude of 7.5, causing immense damage,” Mr. Wijayanto, who, like many Indonesians, goes by one name, said in a statement. He added that the authorities would continue to monitor for aftershocks.

Fathur Rahman, the chief of the search and rescue office in Maumere, one of the largest towns on Flores Island, said his team had confirmed 20 deaths and was still searching for people who could be buried under rubble.

Indonesia, an archipelago with about 17,500 islands, is at the edge of the Pacific Ocean, in an area known as the Ring of Fire. The region experiences frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions as large blocks of the Earth’s crust collide. More than 2,000 people were killed in 2018 after a 7.5-magnitude earthquake and ensuing tsunami devastated central Indonesia.

The authorities initially issued a tsunami warning on Saturday, but soon after said the threat had passed.

The quake struck about 42 miles northwest of Ende, the regional capital, according to data from the United States Geological Survey. Several aftershocks were reported in the area in the hours after the temblor, including one with a magnitude of 6.1. The authorities warned that more could occur in the coming days.

Rin Hindryati contributed reporting.

item.title: Israeli Strikes in Lebanon Kill 11, Health Officials Say
item.description:
A pair of Israeli strikes killed at least 11 people in southern Lebanon early Saturday, the Lebanese health ministry said, one of the deadliest attacks in the country since a fragile truce took effect nearly two months ago.

A strike overnight in Ansar, near the city of Nabatieh, killed seven people, including three children, and wounded two others, health ministry officials said. Hours later, Israeli warplanes carried out an airstrike on Deir al-Zahrani, killing at least four and wounding 17 others, according to the ministry.

The Israeli military said in a statement that its attacks in the Ansar area had targeted infrastructure belonging to Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group. It did not respond to a request for comment on the reports of civilian deaths or on the attack later on Saturday morning.

Nawaf Salam, Lebanon’s prime minister, called the escalation on Saturday “extremely dangerous” and said it undermined efforts to establish stability in the country’s south.

“The seven martyrs in the Israeli strike on Ansar town were not ‘military infrastructure,’ and the children and women killed were not military targets,” Mr. Nawaf said on social media.

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said later on Saturday that Hezbollah had attacked Israeli soldiers inside Lebanon, seriously injuring three of them. The military, it said in a statement, then struck the group’s “headquarters which ordered the attack” and only later learned “that Hezbollah deliberately put civilians in that military compound.”

When approached for comment, a Hezbollah spokesman denied that claim. The group condemned the attacks in a separate statement, accusing Mr. Netanyahu of escalating the war “in order to strengthen his domestic political position.” The group vowed that the strikes would be “met with an appropriate response.”

A cease-fire reached in mid-June was meant to halt the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah and pave the way for establishing a more durable peace. But the truce has since frayed, with fighting between the two sides continuing across southern Lebanon.

The strikes on Saturday come as Israel and Lebanon remain at odds over the terms of a “framework agreement” that was intended to wind down the conflict after months of U.S.-mediated negotiations in Washington and Rome.

Under the agreement, signed on June 26, Israel is expected to gradually withdraw from territory it occupies in southern Lebanon, and the Lebanese Armed Forces would then deploy in those areas and help facilitate the return of residents displaced by the fighting.

The framework has been criticized in Lebanon because it does not set out a timetable for the Israeli withdrawal, and because it links the process to the Lebanese government’s efforts to disarm Hezbollah, which the state has long struggled to do.

Hezbollah itself was not a party to the U.S.-brokered negotiations and has rejected direct talks with Israel.

In a statement published online by his office on Saturday, Lebanon’s president, Joseph Aoun, condemned “Israel’s repeated violations of the framework agreement” along with the “international laws requiring the protection of civilians.”

The war in Lebanon began in early March after Hezbollah fired into Israel in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. The subsequent fighting has killed more than 4,300 people and wounded more than 12,000, according to Lebanon’s health ministry. More than one million people have been displaced as Lebanon’s economic and humanitarian crises have deepened, according to the International Organization for Migration.

Israel has continued to occupy swaths of southern Lebanon. In recent weeks, it has demolished buildings in areas it controls and carried out sporadic attacks in the south, including airstrikes and drone strikes, according to Lebanese officials and state media. The Israeli military says the operations aim to dismantle Hezbollah infrastructure and prevent the group from rearming and threatening northern Israel.

As part of their attack early Saturday, Israeli forces blew up buildings in the southern town of Bint Jbeil and several nearby villages, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported.

Israel marks the boundary of the area it controls on its maps, and says that it considers any armed person operating south of that demarcation line as a security threat and a legitimate military target.

In a televised speech on Friday, Hezbollah’s leader, Naim Qassem, condemned the recent Israeli strikes, saying they demonstrated the futility of negotiating with Israel. He also criticized the pace and manner of the Israeli withdrawal, and the difficulties faced by the Lebanese Army in taking control of those areas and enabling displaced residents to return.

“These negotiations will bring nothing but shame and disgrace,” Mr. Qassem said.

Hwaida Saad, Aaron Boxerman and Sarah Chaayto contributed reporting.

item.title: Iran Says Qatar Captured Three of Its Pilots Early in War With U.S.
item.description:
Iran has accused Qatar of capturing three of its bomber pilots in the early days of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, and on Saturday called on the International Committee of the Red Cross to intervene on their behalf.

Gen. Seyed Mohammad Bagherzadeh, commander of the Iranian armed forces’ missing persons search committee, wrote to the global aid organization in a letter published by Iranian media. He said the men were flying Su-24 fighter jets in an operation on March 2, days after the outbreak of the war, when their planes had been hit by “enemy defenses” and the pilots ejected.

They survived but were captured by the Qatari authorities, according to General Bagherzadeh, who named the men as Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian and Omran Behraveshian. A fourth pilot, Majid Kazemi, died, he added.

The Red Cross and a Qatari government spokesman did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

General Bagherzadeh’s letter was the most precise indication so far of what Iran believes happened to the three pilots. Before Saturday’s letter, Iranian authorities had said the fate of the men was unknown.

Qatar, a close U.S. ally that hosts a major American military base, said on March 2 that its Air Force had shot down two Iranian Su-24 bomber jets. Iran lashed out at its Persian Gulf neighbors soon after it was attacked by the United States and Israel.

Qatar “has not allowed the prisoners to meet or speak with their families or with officials handling their cases,” General Bagherzadeh wrote. He called on the Red Cross to meet with the pilots, investigate their condition, and facilitate their release as soon as possible.

Aaron Boxerman contributed reporting.

item.title: Wary of Trump, Europe Seeks Role in Any Russia-Ukraine Talks
item.description:
Nervous about being excluded by President Trump from any talks to end the Russia-Ukraine war, three European countries are working together to make sure Europe has a seat at the table, according to five European officials.

European diplomats are working on a format for future negotiations to protect European interests that would be led by France, Germany and Britain.

France and Germany are taking the lead in developing the European position, according to two senior European diplomats and a senior European official monitoring the effort. Britain, which has a new prime minister, is more hesitant, in part because it is nervous about testing its relations with Mr. Trump, the diplomats said.

There is little indication that President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia is ready for serious negotiations. The Europeans expect that any negotiation with Russia over Ukraine would be led by the United States, and as Russia is increasing its ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian civilians, they are pushing for Mr. Trump and his envoys to re-engage with Moscow.

But a Ukraine settlement and relations with Russia are too important to Europe to be outsourced indefinitely to a Trump administration that appears increasingly unpredictable, said the officials, all of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue. They want to ensure no deal is cut over their heads by Washington and Moscow.

Western officials and analysts expect the war to become more destructive as Mr. Putin presses for a winter offensive against Ukrainian lines and civilian infrastructure as Ukraine runs severely short of air defenses. Some expect Mr. Putin to order a modest if unpopular mobilization of new troops, but only after parliamentary elections in mid-September. And some even worry that Mr. Putin, feeling cornered, might try to escalate the war and test the solidarity of NATO, beyond hybrid attacks in Europe.

Mr. Putin has said that Russia must at the least obtain complete control over the Donbas region of eastern Ukraine. If the Russians cannot do that by autumn 2027, officials and analysts said, talks would be more likely. And key decisions must be made in advance.

Asked for comment, the British Foreign Office said the discussion remained speculative, while an E.U. official insisted that various diplomatic efforts were complementary rather than competitive, and that a divisive discussion about representation now was not helpful.

For Europe, the stakes are enormous. Ukraine is a major security challenge, and a Russian victory there would have huge consequences. At the same time, Mr. Trump has made it clear that Ukraine is a European responsibility. Europe is already funding Ukraine’s war, and it is expected to provide security assurances to Ukraine after any settlement. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine “wants Europe at the table,” said Alexander Gabuev, the director of the research institute Carnegie Russia.

The 27-member European Union, which has passed 21 sets of sanctions against Russia and possesses the bulk of Russia’s frozen assets, would need to play a role. Both issues would be central to any diplomatic solution.

Britain, France and Germany believe they should be the core negotiators in support of Ukraine, three European officials said. The three countries, known as the “E3,” are the heart of the “coalition of the willing” supporting Ukraine and have drawn up options for military and security guarantees for the country after a settlement.

Poland, Italy and the Nordic countries must also be consulted and the European Union kept informed and later involved, the officials said, because some smaller countries, particularly those neighboring Russia and Ukraine, like the Baltic States and Hungary, do not fully trust Germany and France to represent their interests.

There was a flurry of meetings and debate around the issue in June as Mr. Zelensky pushed to prepare for talks with Russia and the United States.

Mr. Zelensky had reached out to Britain, France and Germany and met their leaders in London on June 7 to discuss the European role in future negotiations with Russia and to set out principles for any agreement. Four days later, the ambassadors of the three European countries had an unusual meeting in Moscow with Mikhail Y. Galuzin, a Russian deputy foreign minister who handles Ukraine.

Kaja Kallas, the E.U. foreign-policy chief, acknowledged Mr. Zelensky’s outreach to Britain, France and Germany and said that the three were respecting “European core security interests,” including sanctions relief and the unfreezing of Russian assets. It was still too early to be definitive about representation, she said, but those core interests had to be heeded.

The European Union then made some tentative steps to open channels with Russia after Mr. Zelensky asked António Costa, the president of the bloc’s intergovernmental body, the European Council, to raise Ukraine with Moscow. Mr. Costa’s chief of staff, Pedro Lourtie, spoke with Russian officials including Yuri V. Ushakov, who has been the main Russian contact for Mr. Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, to try to open up a diplomatic channel.

“We cannot depend only on others to interpret Russian messages, and we must be able to convey directly to Russia our own messages,” Mr. Costa said after a European meeting June 19. But he conceded there were no “credible signs” from Moscow that it wanted to engage in “serious negotiations for the time being.”

In both cases, the official Russian response was dismissive, with Mr. Galuzin complaining that the three countries were “pushing Ukraine to continue the war against Russia.”

Inevitably, Mr. Costa’s outreach provoked divisions, with both France and Germany criticizing him for overreaching, Austria and Belgium supporting him, and the Baltic nations dismissing any approach to Moscow as playing into Russia’s hands.

President Emmanuel Macron of France, for his part, said that “when there are negotiations, the Europeans will have to be around the table,” and that “President Costa, within the competencies defined for him, will have a place.”

Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany emphasized that the three nations were acting “at the express request of Ukraine.” He added: “It also makes a certain internal logic that Britain, Germany and France are working closely together here; these are major European states, and they are also the ones contributing significantly to Ukraine’s military support.”

As for who would speak for the European Union, he said, “We will decide that when talks take place.”

Given Mr. Putin’s lack of interest, Europeans are engaged in wishful thinking, said Norbert Röttgen, a German legislator and security expert. “At some point Europe must be there, because European security is at stake and is no longer seen by Washington as a vital American interest,” he said.

“But for now,” Mr. Röttgen continued, “Putin sees an advantage in trying to divide the West and handle Europe through Washington.”

Others see a European approach to Russia as long overdue. The stakes are so high that Europe’s lack of direct channels to Russia since it invaded Ukraine in 2022 “is almost a criminal dereliction of duty,” said Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, a research institute.

Hans-Dieter Lucas, a former German diplomat who has served as ambassador to NATO, France and Italy, said that there were lessons from the multinational talks with Iran over the 2015 nuclear deal, which he helped to negotiate.

“We cannot be behind the curve as we were” in November 2025, when Mr. Trump and Mr. Witkoff came up with their initial 28-point “peace plan” with Moscow, he said. “The Europeans have cards, but we need to play them smartly.”

Still, Mr. Lucas said, “We will need very close cooperation and coordination with the United States — otherwise the Russians drive wedges between us.” And here, he added, “We are back to the fundamental question of Mr. Trump and the trans-Atlantic relationship.”

Jeanna Smialek contributed reporting from Brussels.

item.title: Canadian Petition to Expel U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra Takes Off
item.description:
After boycotting American products and shunning vacations south of the border, Canadians in their thousands are pouring their incandescent anger at the United States into a new cause: ousting the American ambassador.

More than 160,000 people have signed a petition to the Canadian Parliament, submitted by a Calgary resident on July 21, calling for the removal of the ambassador, Pete Hoekstra.

The petition asserts that Mr. Hoekstra, a faithful messenger of President Trump’s aggressive stance toward Canada, has harmed U.S.-Canada relations. The two countries are locked in a trade war, and their relationship, once the closest two nations can be, has been at a historic low since Mr. Trump retook office.

Just 500 signatures are legally required to bring an online petition to the Parliament floor for discussion, and this one will most likely be put forward for debate in the fall by Elizabeth May, the leader of Canada’s Green Party.

The petition lays out the reasoning for Mr. Hoekstra’s removal: it argues that he has “normalized the Trump administration’s threats to annex Canada as the 51st state.” Mr. Hoekstra has reposted Mr. Trump’s 51st-state jabs on social media and has dismissed Canadians’ anger at the rhetoric as “emotional” and inexplicable.

It also states that Mr. Hoekstra has interfered in Canadian politics in a manner “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol.” It lays out how activists from Alberta seeking to break away from the rest of the country repeatedly met with State Department officials, “raising serious questions about U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian unity.”

The petition calls on the Canadian government to invoke the Vienna Convention of Diplomatic Relations, the international accord that governs diplomacy, declare Mr. Hoekstra “persona non grata” and request his removal from office, as well as to set up a parliamentary committee to review “U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs."

The United States Embassy in Ottawa referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The petition culminates months of souring public sentiment toward Mr. Hoekstra personally, mirroring the plummeting views toward the United States generally.

Polling shows Canadians’ opinion of the United States has rapidly gotten worse since Mr. Trump took office and began targeting Canada with tariffs and talk of making it part of the United States. A Pew survey published in June found that only 35 percent of Canadians now view the United States as a reliable partner, down sharply from 2022, when it was 82 percent. Canadian recreational visits to the United States have shrunk by more than a quarter over the past year.

In this context, Mr. Hoekstra, a former Republican Representative from Michigan, has become notorious in Canada for his blunt, unapologetic tone, which channels Mr. Trump’s.

One comment that drew ire came in November, when Mr. Hoekstra was asked if he understood why Canadians found Mr. Trump’s 51st state remarks upsetting.

“Here, I’ll just get myself in trouble,” he said. “I go around the country and people will say, ‘Pete, you just don’t understand why we’re so mad about the 51st state.’ Yeah, you’re right. I don’t.”

Unlike some of his colleagues, Mr. Hoekstra has never been summoned by the Canadian government, a step taken when a diplomatic emissary is seen as overstepping so badly that the host government needs to give them a talking-to.

The United States ambassador to France, Charles Kushner, the father of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared, has been twice summoned by the French government over comments he has made about French domestic affairs. The U.S. ambassador to Belgium was also summoned for comments he made.

Mr. Hoekstra also raised eyebrows when he invited the right-wing populist activist Tamara Lich, who had been convicted of organizing the trucker convoy that wreaked havoc in Ottawa for a month in 2022, to this year’s 4th of July party at the ambassador’s official residence.

Mr. Hoekstra has been accused of political interference in another nation’s domestic affairs. In 2020, while serving as U.S. ambassador to the Netherlands in the first Trump administration, he hosted an event at the U.S. embassy with a nativist, anti-immigrant Dutch party.

Expelling a U.S. ambassador would be a first for Canada, but far from unprecedented globally.

American ambassadors have been expelled during major geopolitical crises in the past, including during the Cold War, both World Wars, as well as more recently during crises with Latin American countries such as Venezuela.

Mr. Hoekstra’s stance in Canada aligns with the U.S. administration’s foreign policy elsewhere. The State Department has made significant efforts to cultivate and promote identarian politics in Europe through visits and senior official meetings with European political parties and other organizations sharing these ideas, including in Germany and Britain.

Representatives of the business community said Mr. Hoekstra had been a solid interlocutor during tumultuous times for the relationship between the two nations.

The U.S. Embassy in Canada recommended speaking to some business leaders about their working relationship with Mr. Hoekstra. They included Rick Tachuk, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Canada, a private, nonprofit membership organization promoting trade and investment across the border; and Beth Burke, chief executive of the Canadian American Business Council, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group.

Mr. Tachuk says that Mr. Hoekstra has been available to business leaders and cares about the U.S.-Canada trade relationship.

“He at times can be blunt, but, in many respects, that is an advantage for us because he helps articulate the view of the president, and helps us understand what the challenges are,” Mr. Tachuk said in an interview on Friday.

“Ambassador Hoekstra has to deliver some very unpopular messages here in Canada. It’s a tough job but he’s doing his best,” he added.

Ms. Burke said Mr. Hoekstra was well connected across the administration and an effective messenger.

“I also really value knowing where you stand in a situation. Sometimes pleasantries and diplomatic speak muddy the waters,” she added.

item.title: Syrian Convicted in Austria of Civil War Abuses Is Detained in Syria
item.description:
When a court in Vienna last month convicted two former Syrian officials of abuses during their country’s civil war, the case was celebrated as a groundbreaking pursuit of justice for victims of the fallen Syrian dictatorship.

But weeks later, one of those convicted, Musab Abu Rukbah, a former police chief, left Austria and traveled back to Syria after appealing his eight-year sentence. Now the Syrian government has announced that it has arrested him.

Syria’s Internal Security Forces said on Saturday that they had detained Mr. Abu Rukbah as part of “ongoing security operations to prosecute those involved in terrorism cases and take the necessary legal action against them.” The arrest came after reports that he had returned to his hometown, Nawa, in the southern province of Daraa.

Mr. Abu Rukbah, 54, had not been deemed a flight risk by a higher court in Vienna and was free while the appeal process was underway, Christina Salzborn, the vice president of the Regional Court of Vienna, said earlier this month.

Mr. Abu Rukbah had been released without conditions after a brief detention at the time of his indictment in January 2025, and he was not under any reporting requirements, travel ban or obligation to surrender his passport, Ms. Salzborn said.

But earlier this month, after Syrian activists posted on social media that they had learned of Mr. Abu Rukbah’s return, a lawyer representing victims in the case against him said she had applied for an international arrest warrant. The lawyer, Tatiana Urdaneta Wittek, is the director of the Center for the Enforcement of Human Rights International, a nonprofit organization in Vienna.

Ms. Urdaneta Wittek said this month that Mr. Abu Rukbah’s return to Syria was grounds enough for an arrest warrant to be issued, though she also noted that Syria does not have an extradition treaty with Austria. A hearing date for Mr. Abu Rukbah’s appeal had not been set.

“With his escape to Syria, he is withdrawing from the proceedings before they are final,” Ms. Urdaneta Wittek said.

The court in Austria has made no public announcement about any warrant for Mr. Abu Rukbah’s arrest. Earlier this month, Roman Valach, a lawyer who represented Mr. Abu Rukbah at the trial, declined to comment on his whereabouts.

Ms. Urdaneta Wittek and Mr. Valach could not immediately be reached for comment on Saturday after the announcement of Mr. Abu Rukbah’s arrest.

His return home is a test for Syria’s government, which is struggling to deliver justice for the hundreds of thousands of victims of the country’s civil war, 18 months after overthrowing the dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad.

Ms. Urdaneta Wittek’s application for a warrant, which was seen by The New York Times, said that an investigative group specializing in international justice cases, Arctic Wind Solutions, had confirmed with the Syrian border authorities that Mr. Abu Rukbah had crossed into Syria early on the morning of July 29.

Mr. Abu Rukbah’s apparent escape was an embarrassment for the Austrian authorities and a blow to his many victims after a 10-year investigation of him and a former intelligence official, Khaled al-Halabi.

Asyad Almousa, who was among those who testified against Mr. Abu Rukbah in Vienna, said before the announcement of his arrest that a whole new case now had to be built in Syria. “We are starting from zero,” he said, “which means years more of agonizing judicial process.”

Mr. Abu Rukbah and Mr. al-Halabi had claimed asylum in Austria after arriving in 2015, several years after the start of Syria’s civil war. They were convicted, in a rarity there, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows a country to prosecute individuals for grave crimes committed elsewhere.

Twenty Syrian survivors testified against the two former officials during the trial, describing harrowing details of lasting physical and psychological trauma at their hands.

Mr. al-Halabi was convicted of torture and other crimes. Mr. Abu Rukbah was convicted on charges that included aggravated coercion and sexual coercion. Both men were sentenced to eight years in prison and lodged appeals through their lawyers.

“I feel a deep sadness seeing this happen,” said Mr. Almousa, the victim who had testified against Mr. Abu Rukbah. “Years of demanding our rights went into the wind because of the Austrian justice system’s carelessness. How was a man sentenced to eight years let go, free and not monitored?”

Naz Kucuktekin contributed reporting from Vienna.

item.title: The Iranian YouTube Show Posing Questions Few Dare Ask
item.description:
When the conservative American commentator Tucker Carlson sat down last year for a buzzy interview with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, the unlikely encounter would most likely never have happened without the involvement of a tiny, independent Iranian outlet.

Mahdi Ahmadi, the founder of Azad, a six-person team that hosts debates in Tehran and publishes them on YouTube, pitched Mr. Carlson on the idea, he said, and then connected him with the president’s team.

This mediating role is a tightrope that Mr. Ahmadi and his team have become adept at walking over the past few years. Their YouTube channel has aired views that are deeply critical of Iran’s government, alongside those of people close to the authorities, attracting a large and growing online audience, as well as scrutiny and criticism.

Mr. Carlson did not respond to a request for comment for this article, but his channel did thank Mr. Ahmadi for his help at the end of the Pezeshkian interview.

Mr. Ahmadi, 35, said in an interview with The New York Times that he saw Azad’s role as sitting between two opposing sides and creating a chance for mutual understanding — and allowing viewers to judge each side’s arguments for themselves.

“We believe that, for the future of Iranian society, this is essential,” he said.

Crucial to Azad’s approach is Mr. Ahmadi’s studious impartiality as a moderator. He has described the channel as a neutral “court of ideas” where viewers could be exposed to, and assess, an ideologically diverse set of perspectives.

This year, Azad hosted a debate in which one scholar advocated an end to Iran’s Islamic government via a constitutional referendum. Another went further — arguing for the return of the country’s exiled monarchy. Weeks earlier, Iranian security forces had killed thousands of antigovernment protesters, some of whom were calling for the return of the former crown prince, Reza Pahlavi.

Critics of the channel question how Azad has been allowed to continue working inside Iran, given the censorship and control that the state exerts over the media. Many assert that it must have protection from a powerful patron, which Mr. Ahmadi denies.

For the Iranian government, having a program like Azad inside Iran presents some benefits. State television, which has a monopoly on domestic airwaves, is controlled by hard-liners, and millions of Iranians instead get their news and entertainment from overseas Persian-language outlets, which can be stridently antigovernment.

By allowing some discourse within Iran, the government can attempt to dilute the influence of diaspora outlets while it also tries to shape those discussions.

Yet Azad (meaning “free” in Persian) has itself faced pressure from the state. Its website is blocked by the government, and Mr. Ahmadi said the authorities had interrogated him several times. During the June 2025 U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran, the authorities seized Azad’s equipment for 25 days, after it aired two programs about the conflict, Mr. Ahmadi said.

The channel has survived so far, he said, because of its refusal to take up an activist stance, and its balanced cast of guests, ranging from politicians to members of the opposition.

YouTube is also blocked by the government in Iran, but many people circumvent the ban using virtual private networks (VPNs). Mr. Ahmadi estimates that around 70 percent of his channel’s audience is inside Iran, though it is difficult to know for sure because VPNs can mask a person’s location.

The government has also cut off access to the internet for long periods this year, amid mass protests and war, disrupting the ability of Iranian YouTube creators to air new episodes.

Today, Azad has almost 160,000 subscribers, and its videos regularly receive six-figure viewerships. It is funded by crowdfunding and YouTube ads, according to Mr. Ahmadi, who has made open calls for donations to pay the bills.

Azad’s evenhanded approach is rare in Iranian media, in which news outlets are often aligned with political factions and some members of the opposition view traditional journalistic objectivity as a favor toward Iran’s government.

Mr. Ahmadi said it would be impossible for him to fully satisfy those suspicious of Azad.

The only effective answer, he said, was to show “over the long term that one can host diverse voices as much as possible, help increase their visibility and ultimately ask citizens to make use of whatever is valuable to them.”

Azad’s roots stretch back over a decade. From 2014, Mr. Ahmadi organized in-person debates in a project called the Azad Fekri School (the School of Free Thought). The events were held at Tehran’s Sharif University of Technology, where he studied physics.

The discussions covered issues core to Iran’s state ideology, including compulsory hijab and “velayat-e faqih,” the political theory underpinning the system of clerical rule. Mr. Ahmadi has said he wanted opposing sides to talk to each other — not in raucous, gladiatorial debates, but in sober, lengthy presentations of each perspective, followed by dialogue.

It was a rare phenomenon in a country where the theocratic government has harshly punished those who question its ideology, and where even members of the opposition have grown impatient with each other, slinging insults back and forth online.

The debates set off controversy, and the university stopped allowing Azad Fekri School to use its facilities, Mr. Ahmadi said. Sharif University of Technology did not respond to a request for comment.

In 2022, the Azad team pivoted to YouTube. At the time, Iran was in the middle of the Woman, Life, Freedom protests, weeks of demonstrations prompted by the death of a woman in the custody of the morality police. Azad launched a series of conversations on the future of Iran, and the videos took off in popularity.

Since shifting online, Azad has hosted conversations with people who have fallen foul of the authorities, including an Iranian historian convicted and imprisoned under accusations of apostasy and the daughter of a former president who was jailed for her statements against the government. The American intellectual Noam Chomsky used his interview to speak of the need to “free Iranian society from the harsh, cruel, repressive clerical stranglehold of the clerical regime.”

Azad has also invited people onto the show who have positions in line with the government, including a cleric who led a body charged with promoting public morality, and analysts who advise Iran’s decision makers.

Mostafa Najafi, an analyst close to Iran’s security policy circles who has appeared on Azad, said the program stood out for hosting guests with deep expertise. And, with debates commonly stretching to two or more hours, it gave them time to fully lay out their arguments, he said.

Abolfazl Hajizadegan, an Iranian sociologist, appeared on the program last year and criticized the government.

“I didn’t see any attempt to steer me or tell me to hold back,” he said. “That doesn’t mean they don’t have red lines, but in this difficult environment where producing content is hard, they show a degree of courage.”

That willingness to take risks is in part a keen business strategy. If the channel’s producers give in to self-censorship, their project is bound to fail, Mr. Ahmadi said on Tabaghe 16, a Persian-language podcast airing from Canada. “Who would watch it?” he said.

Still, some observers remain skeptical of Azad’s work and motivations.

After decades of government repression, there is some exhaustion in Iran with calls for civility. The kind of respectful dialogue that Azad encourages has fallen out of fashion in some quarters of society.

Azad’s YouTube channel appears to show that, of more than 100 guests over the past year, only four have been women. It has held multiple all-male discussions on the issue of compulsory hijab, a law enforced against women in Iran.

Fatemeh Hassani, a sociologist in Iran, said that the gender imbalance of Azad’s guests reflected its alignment with government interests. After all, she said, women in Iran could speak from experience about the realities of state violence and discrimination.

“The platform wants to project an image of a pluralistic Iranian society, but only a form of pluralism that remains ‘politically safe,’” she said.

Mr. Ahmadi acknowledged that women were underrepresented on the show. He said that Azad regularly invited women to appear, but that they sometimes declined because they face greater political risk, their appearances are harshly scrutinized online, and they tend to be stricter about sticking to their areas of expertise than men.

For Mr. Hajizadegan, it is simplistic to argue that if a media platform is operating in Iran, it must be serving the regime. Even today, the state faces constraints on how it exercises power and is not the sole actor in Iran’s politics, he said.

“The fact that a media outlet remains open should be seen as good news, not something to suspect,” he said. “Saying this doesn’t preclude criticism. Rather, it opens the door for more serious, substantive critiques.”

Mr. Ahmadi accepts that Azad may fall short, and says that he welcomes critique. But he sees Azad as having already succeeded in pushing the boundaries of public discourse in Iran, a project he regards as vital to the country’s future.

“My agenda is dialogue,” Mr. Ahmadi said. “No political group in Iran can be erased. They must be able to talk to one another.”

Leily Nikounazar contributed reporting.

item.title: Professor’s Death Leaves Behind Hard Questions for Cambridge on Race and Hiring
item.description:
When Cambridge University interviewed Jason Arday for one of the most prestigious sociology positions in the world, he was an early career scholar and underqualified, by the school’s own standards.

Cambridge’s requirements, reviewed by The New York Times, called for “an outstanding research record of international stature” and a “proven successful track record” supervising Ph.D. students. Dr. Arday had a modest publication record and had bounced from one university to the next — not staying long enough to oversee a full three-year-or-more doctorate.

Cambridge hired him anyway in 2023, making him, at 37, the university’s youngest Black professor at a time when the school was under pressure to diversify. In doing so, Cambridge thrust him into the international limelight, giving him a platform at one of the world’s elite universities to champion academic diversity and making him a target for critics.

Dr. Arday was found dead in London on Friday, days after resigning his job amid accusations that he had plagiarized chunks of his papers, embellished parts of his recently published memoir and fabricated aspects of his life story. The controversy exploded along cultural fault lines — race, neurodiversity and academic hiring.

In his Aug. 5 resignation later, he wrote, “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.” He added, “This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.”

His family said that, since starting at Cambridge, Dr. Arday had faced a campaign of scrutiny intended to undermine him. That became too much for him, they said.

Questions about Dr. Arday’s career are unlikely to end with his death, however, because they were as much about Cambridge as they were as about him. The centuries-old alma mater of Isaac Newton, William Wordsworth and kings and queens, Cambridge now faces deep scrutiny about its decision-making, even from its own faculty.

While Dr. Arday was underqualified for his job, he had a remarkable story: a tale of being diagnosed early with autism and having such significant developmental delays that he spent his entire childhood in a special-needs school. In his account, he did not speak until age 11 or read until 18, yet he managed to earn his doctorate and begin giving keynote speeches on the academic circuit. Also, he had run 30 marathons in 35 days for charity, a feat that would have placed him among the world’s elite athletes.

If, in hindsight, elements of Dr. Arday’s story seemed too good to be true, Cambridge ignored repeated warning signs. A review of internal Cambridge documents and interviews with former colleagues and associates shows that, in addition to passing over more experienced candidates for the job, administrators gushed publicly about Dr. Arday’s scholarship and privately disregarded complaints about his work. They declined to investigate plagiarism concerns and accused his critics of a “vile campaign” to discredit him.

Dr. Arday’s claims about not speaking were false, a former classmate and a speech professional who worked with him told The New York Times. His supposedly remarkable trajectory from nonverbal preteen to Ph.D. had no precedent in medical literature, experts in developmental and speech delays say. That should have set off alarm bells for the Cambridge hiring committee, which included a child psychiatrist who had done research on autism, experts said.

Before Dr. Arday’s death, conservative commentators seized on his fall as evidence of diversity-and-inclusion efforts run amok. They said that Cambridge had been so eager to diversify that administrators let their judgment be clouded.

“They seem to have drunk the D.E.I. Kool-Aid,” Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former Conservative lawmaker in Britain, said early this week on The Telegraph’s “Daily T” podcast.

Prominent academics on the left agree that Cambridge must answer for its decisions. They say that the ordeal has fueled racism and cast unjustified aspersions on accomplished scholars of color.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was “desperately saddened” to hear of Dr. Arday’s death. An administrator, in a letter to the faculty on Tuesday, called the misconduct accusations “an aberration” and “troubling.” A spokesman separately declined to answer a list of questions about his hiring and his time there, citing a planned independent investigation — a difficult inquiry that will likely be made even more uncomfortable following Dr. Arday’s death.

Dr. Arday, for his part, had worked hard to silence any questioning of his credentials. When a journalist for Times Higher Education, a respected academic industry publication, asked about plagiarism last year, a prominent British defamation law firm helped kill the article, the journalist said. Dr. Arday later reported the journalist to the police.

When a scholar from another university questioned his work, Dr. Arday turned the tables and filed a racism complaint with the other school, according to someone with direct knowledge of the complaint. That person, like some others who spoke to The Times, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid being dragged publicly into the controversy.

Dr. Arday never squarely addressed the questions of plagiarism and fabrication.

But what is clear from interviews and public records is that elements of the story would have been easy for Cambridge to check.

Dr. Arday, the child of Ghanaian immigrants, grew up in public housing in an ethnically mixed, working-class quarter of South London. Early on, he was identified as having learning difficulties.

Dr. Arday has claimed that before age 11, he could understand language but not speak. In 2022, before interviewing with Cambridge, he said that he had been educated exclusively in a special-needs school “with other pupils that had very severe learning difficulties and physical disabilities.”

In his memoir, published on Tuesday, he gave a different account, saying he attended a mainstream school but spent time sequestered alone in a classroom, again without speaking.

Both tales are false, according to people who knew Dr. Arday as a child and spoke with The Times before his death.

A speech professional who worked closely with the young Dr. Arday recalled him having a language delay but speaking with both children and adults.

One former schoolmate, Jonathan Stewart, recalled Dr. Arday cracking jokes and putting on playful accents in a minivan on the way to church activities as children.

While nonverbal children can certainly learn to speak, even at a late age, the rapid development described by Dr. Arday has no precedent in clinical literature, three experts on autism and speech said.

“In over 40 years of practice and being very acquainted with literature, I’ve never heard of that happening,” said Stephen Camarata, a speech science expert with Vanderbilt Health’s Developmental Disabilities Lab. “It just stretches credulity.”

An established chair at Cambridge, a permanently funded position that comes with prestige and research support, is among the academic world’s most sought-after jobs.

Dr. Arday applied for an established chair of education at Jesus College, one of Cambridge’s oldest institutions, dating to the 15th century. The university advertised internationally for the job and convened a panel of nine experts to review the candidates.

The panel selected four finalists, inviting them to Cambridge for two days of interviews. Dr. Arday was up against three more senior scholars, including two women of color, according to a person familiar with the hiring process.

Dr. Arday’s published papers and his thesis had dozens of grammatical errors, along with identical quotes attributed to different people.

At Cambridge, the finalists were asked to submit just one piece of research, according to the person familiar with the process.

It is not clear which piece he submitted, or whether members of the hiring panel reviewed Dr. Arday’s speeches and interviews. If they had, they would have found elements of his story that stretched belief, like the marathon claim, or were demonstrably false, like his public assertion that he had been on the British television series “Seven Up.” (Dr. Arday’s spokesman recently said that the assertion should not have been taken literally.)

Experts said that Cambridge’s hiring panel was well equipped to question Dr. Arday’s very public claims about his childhood. Some committee members had published papers about teaching students with learning disabilities and about inclusion in education.

One influential member of the hiring panel, the child psychiatrist Paul Ramchandani, had published a paper on music therapy for children with autism. Given his expertise, he would have been in position to question Dr. Arday’s assertion that he learned to speak at 11 and read at 18, said Howard Shane, the director emeritus of the Center for Communication Enhancement at Boston Children’s Hospital.

“That should raise a red flag,” he said in an interview early this week. “There’s no question about that.”

Dr. Ramchandani and others on the panel did not respond to requests for comment.

The committee hired Dr. Arday, in a decision that the education department chair described at the time as unanimous. Cambridge’s lengthy hiring announcement highlighted his remarkable personal story, which garnered media coverage on both sides of the Atlantic.

Cambridge had so few Black professors that it was under pressure from faculty and students to diversify. It had set modest targets for increasing applications from people of color for academic posts.

On the BBC, the education department chair, Hilary Cremin, told Dr. Arday that he was “the best in the world in terms of the research you do.” She did not respond to requests for comment.

Three months after Dr. Arday’s hiring, two British scholars, Martyn Hammersley and David Harris, privately wrote to Cambridge, alerting administrators to potential plagiarism in one of Dr. Arday’s papers.

Dr. Cremin, the department chair, replied that she had met with Dr. Arday, and that he had agreed to address concerns in the paper. She also mentioned his “ongoing experiences of direct and indirect racism,” along with “significant health issues” that had affected his work on the paper in question, according to an email, which was first reported on a former professor’s newsletter and the academic integrity website Retraction Watch.

Dr. Harris, whose work has challenged whether racism is ingrained in society, responded by suggesting that Cambridge also review Dr. Arday’s other papers and his thesis. “Prof Arday badly needs critical friends, in my view, not sycophants,” he wrote.

He never got a reply, he said.

Nor did Cambridge act months later after journals appended corrections on two of Dr. Arday’s papers. Then, in September 2025, Times Higher Education sent Cambridge a dossier of more than 60 pages that detailed apparent plagiarism in Dr. Arday’s work.

A reporter and editor at the publication, Jack Grove, had enlisted experts to review Dr. Arday’s thesis.

One of them, David Sanders of Purdue University, told The Times that, going into the review, he knew nothing about Jason Arday. But when Dr. Sanders sat down to analyze the thesis, he concluded it was “extensively plagiarized.”

Cambridge continued to back its star professor, telling Mr. Grove that questions about Dr. Arday’s thesis would have to be addressed by the school that had awarded his doctorate, Liverpool John Moores University. Concerns about his research, Cambridge said, would similarly have to be handled by others. Liverpool John Moores stood by his doctorate.

At Cambridge, faculty members and allies hurriedly drafted a letter in anticipation of Mr. Grove’s article. “The integrity of higher education is at risk if we do not take a stand and speak out against the systematic attempts to erase Black scholarship,” they wrote in the letter, a copy of which was seen by The Times.

But Mr. Grove’s article never ran. Dr. Arday’s lawyers threatened legal action, and Times Higher Education spiked it. Dr. Arday also filed a police complaint against Mr. Grove, which led to a harassment investigation that was later dropped.

The plagiarism charges burst into public view last month when a former Cambridge scholar, Nathan Cofnas, wrote about them in his newsletter. Dr. Cofnas is known for his work suggesting that Black people were genetically predisposed to be less intelligent than white people. The university had cut ties with him in 2024.

Retraction Watch quickly expanded on Dr. Cofnas’s reporting. But once again, Cambridge defended Dr. Arday, saying he was “the victim of a vile campaign to undermine his credibility, which must stop,” according to an email seen by The Times.

After new questions surfaced, casting doubt on Dr. Arday’s story, he resigned. Cambridge’s tone shifted.

But the fallout from Cambridge’s enthusiastic promotion of Dr. Arday’s story could last for years. “This has really done some harm,” Dr. Camarata, the speech specialist, said before Dr. Arday’s death.

He said that over the years, he heard from families of children with severe autism hoping for a miracle. “I never want to take away anybody’s hope,” he said, “but this story really has created some unreasonable expectations and false hopes, and I hate that.”

Heidi Mirza, an emeritus professor of education at University College London who once mentored Dr. Arday, said in an interview this past week that he had been ill-served by university administrators’ carelessness in their efforts to demonstrate their commitment to diversity.

“He’s a pawn,” she said, “whose ambition made him vulnerable.”

Georgia Gee, Susan C. Beachy and Kitty Bennett contributed research.
